candidates.name: AI Fiduciaries
candidates.source_quote: AI fiduciaries handle sensitive medical data locally, enabling rapid diagnosis and vaccine development while preserving patient privacy. The crisis demonstrates that accountable AI, deployed through federated networks, can coordinate at civilizational scale without centralizing control.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section 2.4 Maturation of Defensive Networks, under '2031: Deployment of AI Fiduciaries'
candidates.one_liner: Locally-deployed AI agents that process sensitive medical data on-site within federated health networks, enabling cross-network coordination without centralizing raw data.
candidates.mechanism: Each AI fiduciary operates within a local node (e.g., a hospital or regional lab), processing patient data in place rather than transmitting it to a central repository. The fiduciaries coordinate diagnosis and vaccine development outputs across the federated network by sharing results and models rather than raw data. This preserves patient privacy while enabling civilizational-scale crisis response without any single entity controlling the underlying data.
candidates.exists_today: Partial implementations exist in federated learning frameworks and privacy-preserving computation (e.g., secure enclaves, differential privacy in health research), but the specific framing of an 'AI fiduciary' as an accountable, locally-deployed agent with defined custodial responsibilities within a federated crisis-response mesh is not a standardized deployed system.
candidates.source_section: 2.1 How We Got Here: The Path to d/acc 2035

candidates.name: Interoperable Governance Protocol Stack
candidates.source_quote: A coalition of federated city-states launches the first interoperable governance protocol stack, allowing citizens to carry digital IDs, benefits, and credentials between different local systems. When severe flooding hits multiple jurisdictions, modular governance systems coordinate relief in hours instead of weeks, sharing resources and logistics seamlessly across local and regional levels.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section 2.5 Stress Testing, under '2033: The Interoperability Breakthrough'
candidates.one_liner: A shared technical and governance protocol layer that allows citizens to port digital identities, benefits, and credentials across distinct federated city-state systems, and enables AI systems across those jurisdictions to align resource allocation and crisis modeling.
candidates.mechanism: The protocol stack defines common standards for digital identity, benefits entitlements, and credentials so that any compliant local system can read and honor records issued by another. During crises, the same stack enables federated AI systems across jurisdictions to share resource allocation decisions, risk assessments, and logistics data in a machine-readable, interoperable format. Governance modules are modular, so jurisdictions can adopt the stack without surrendering local policy autonomy, and the protocol layer handles translation between differing local implementations.
candidates.exists_today: Partial analogues exist in eIDAS (EU digital identity interoperability), W3C Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs), and Verifiable Credentials standards, but none combine cross-jurisdictional civic benefits portability with an AI coordination layer for real-time crisis resource allocation at the described scale.
candidates.source_section: 2.1 How We Got Here: The Path to d/acc 2035

candidates.name: Federated Procurement Platforms
candidates.source_quote: Federated procurement platforms let mid-sized buyers pool resources, but uneven coordination leaves some regions overstocked, others empty.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section 2.2 The Reality Check, under '2027: The Supply Chain Cascade'
candidates.one_liner: A federated platform allowing mid-sized institutional buyers (hospitals, utilities, manufacturers) to pool purchasing power and coordinate supply acquisition across a distributed network rather than through a single centralized marketplace.
candidates.mechanism: Mid-sized buyers join a federated network where each node represents an institution or cooperative. The platform aggregates demand signals across nodes to negotiate collective purchasing, then distributes allocations according to local need. AI-assisted coordination matches supply availability to regional demand in real time, with the goal of preventing large buyers from monopolizing scarce goods. Interoperability standards allow nodes running different local systems to participate in the same procurement events.
candidates.exists_today: Group purchasing organizations (GPOs) in healthcare and government procurement consortia exist, but a federated, AI-assisted, interoperable version spanning diverse institutional types and jurisdictions with real-time allocation is not a deployed standard system.
candidates.source_section: 2.1 How We Got Here: The Path to d/acc 2035

candidates.name: Jurisdictional Routers
candidates.source_quote: Protocols that mediate between state law and DAO bylaws, clarifying authority and handling disputes at the interface of centralized and decentralized systems. These systems are economically sustainable through transaction fees, creating self-funding infrastructure for managing jurisdictional complexity.
candidates.source_quote_context: Governance section, 'What's in use in 2035' subsection
candidates.one_liner: Self-funding protocol layer that mediates legal authority disputes between nation-state law and DAO governance, sustained by transaction fees.
candidates.mechanism: When a conflict arises between state law and DAO bylaws, the Jurisdictional Router protocol adjudicates which authority applies and routes the dispute accordingly. The system charges transaction fees for each mediation, making it financially self-sustaining without public subsidy. This creates persistent infrastructure for managing the interface between centralized and decentralized legal systems.
candidates.exists_today: Kleros offers decentralized dispute resolution; some legal tech platforms handle cross-jurisdictional arbitration, but no self-funding protocol layer specifically mediating state-law/DAO-bylaw conflicts exists.
candidates.source_section: 3 How d/acc Transformed Key Domains Across Society

candidates.name: Safety-Netted DAOs
candidates.source_quote: Civic organizations that retain temporary centralized controls (e.g., a 'circuit breaker' council) to intervene in crises, with clear, time-locked paths toward greater decentralization.
candidates.source_quote_context: Governance section, 'What's in use in 2035' subsection
candidates.one_liner: DAO governance structure with a built-in emergency override council whose authority is automatically time-limited, with a pre-committed schedule for returning to decentralized control.
candidates.mechanism: A civic DAO embeds a small 'circuit breaker' council with authority to override decentralized governance during crises. This centralized override is not permanent: the council's authority is time-locked, meaning it automatically expires after a defined period, and the path back to decentralization is encoded in advance and cannot be unilaterally extended. This prevents emergency powers from becoming permanent while still allowing rapid crisis response.
candidates.exists_today: Some DeFi protocols include emergency pause mechanisms (e.g., multisig admin keys), but these lack the formal time-lock commitment to decentralization re-entry that defines this proposal.
candidates.source_section: 3 How d/acc Transformed Key Domains Across Society

candidates.name: Pareto-Optimal Negotiation Bots
candidates.source_quote: AI systems designed to find mutually beneficial outcomes handle routine commercial negotiations. These systems focus on creating value for both sides and avoid perpetuating existing human biases by learning from outcomes rather than human behavior patterns.
candidates.source_quote_context: Law & Justice section, 'What's in use in 2035' subsection
candidates.one_liner: Commercial negotiation AI that trains on outcome data rather than human negotiation behavior, specifically to avoid replicating human biases while maximizing joint value.
candidates.mechanism: Rather than training on transcripts or patterns of how humans negotiate (which would encode existing power imbalances and biases), these AI systems are trained on negotiation outcomes — what settlements proved mutually beneficial over time. The system searches for Pareto-optimal agreements by modeling the value space for both parties and proposing terms that expand rather than divide the pie. This design choice explicitly breaks the feedback loop between historical human bias and AI recommendation.
candidates.exists_today: AI negotiation tools exist (e.g., Pactum, some procurement bots), but they generally train on human negotiation data; the specific design of outcome-only training to avoid bias propagation is not a standard deployed approach.
candidates.source_section: 3 How d/acc Transformed Key Domains Across Society

candidates.name: AGI Liability Safe Harbor Framework
candidates.source_quote: Liability frameworks targeting the triple intersection could create strong incentives for Tool AI approaches. Such frameworks would impose strict liability, including personal criminal liability for executives, on systems that combine high autonomy, generality, and intelligence, while providing 'safe harbor' protections for systems that lack one or more of these properties.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section 2 'What is Tool AI?', discussion of mechanisms to incentivize Tool AI development over AGI
candidates.one_liner: A tiered legal liability framework that imposes strict (including criminal) liability on AI systems occupying the high-autonomy + high-generality + high-intelligence intersection, while granting safe harbor to systems lacking one or more of these properties.
candidates.mechanism: The framework maps liability exposure to the AGI 'triple intersection' of Autonomy, Generality, and Intelligence. Systems combining all three face strict liability and personal criminal liability for executives. Systems that are high in one or two dimensions but not all three qualify for reduced (fault-based) or safe harbor liability. This creates economic and legal incentives to deliberately constrain at least one dimension, making Tool AI the commercially viable default for high-stakes applications.
candidates.exists_today: Product liability and sector-specific AI regulations exist (e.g., EU AI Act risk tiers), but none currently impose personal criminal executive liability keyed specifically to the autonomy-generality-intelligence triple intersection as a formal legal trigger.

candidates.name: AI Liability Framework
candidates.source_quote: AI systems cannot be held responsible for their actions, therefore human individuals and organizations must bear full responsibility for harms they cause. The level of liability should reflect the level of risk - systems that combine high autonomy, generality, and intelligence pose the greatest danger and should face the strictest liability standards, including personal criminal liability for executives. However, systems that lack one or more of these properties should receive safe harbor protections under standard fault-based liability.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section 3.1, describing the hypothetical Supreme Court ruling in Regional Health Network v. MedAI Systems, late 2026
candidates.speaker: Report authors (attributed to hypothetical Supreme Court)
candidates.one_liner: A tiered legal liability standard that assigns personal criminal liability to executives of AI systems exhibiting all three of high autonomy, generality, and intelligence, while granting safe harbor to systems lacking any one of those properties.
candidates.mechanism: The framework creates a 'triple intersection' test: if a deployed AI system simultaneously exhibits high autonomy, generality, and intelligence, it falls outside safe harbor and exposes executives to personal criminal liability. Systems that are constrained on any one dimension (e.g., narrow scope or limited autonomy) qualify for safe harbor under standard fault-based liability. Insurance markets reinforce the framework by refusing to underwrite systems in the high-risk triple intersection, making the economic incentive to constrain systems overwhelming.
candidates.exists_today: No equivalent tiered criminal-liability-for-executives framework exists for AI. The EU AI Act creates risk tiers but does not impose personal criminal liability on executives based on a triple-property test.
candidates.source_section: 3 How We Got Here: The Path to a Tool AI World in 2035

candidates.name: contextual autonomy
candidates.source_quote: The most successful approach becomes 'contextual autonomy', systems that automatically reduce their independence based on risk level: autonomous for low-stakes tasks like scheduling, but requiring human oversight for anything involving money, health, or safety.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section 3.1, describing the market pivot of early 2027 as companies adapt to the liability framework
candidates.speaker: Report authors
candidates.one_liner: An AI architecture that dynamically and automatically scales down its own operational autonomy in proportion to the assessed risk level of the task at hand.
candidates.mechanism: The system continuously evaluates the risk category of each pending action and applies a corresponding autonomy tier: fully autonomous execution for low-stakes tasks (e.g., scheduling), mandatory human approval gates for medium-risk tasks, and full human direction for anything touching money, health, or safety. The risk classification and autonomy reduction happen at runtime without requiring separate system deployments, allowing a single model to serve across risk levels while remaining within liability safe harbors.
candidates.exists_today: Partial implementations exist in the form of human-in-the-loop checkpoints in some enterprise AI workflows, but no standardized runtime risk-classification-to-autonomy-reduction architecture is in widespread production deployment.
candidates.source_section: 3 How We Got Here: The Path to a Tool AI World in 2035

candidates.name: Tool AI for Tool AI
candidates.source_quote: Tool AI for Tool AI emerges: interpretable AI systems help design and validate other interpretable AI systems, creating scalable oversight mechanisms.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section 3.2, describing the technical foundation period of 2027-2028
candidates.speaker: Report authors
candidates.one_liner: A recursive oversight architecture in which interpretable, constrained AI systems are used to design, audit, and validate other interpretable AI systems, scaling human oversight without requiring proportional human labor.
candidates.mechanism: Interpretable Tool AI systems are deployed as validators and designers of other Tool AI systems, checking that candidate systems meet interpretability, audit-trail, and autonomy-constraint standards before deployment. Because the validating systems are themselves interpretable and human-overseen, the chain of oversight remains auditable at each level. This allows the volume of AI systems being deployed to grow faster than the human workforce capable of manually reviewing each one.
candidates.exists_today: Related concepts exist in AI safety research (e.g., scalable oversight, debate, and recursive reward modeling), and RAND has written on AI automating AI R&D, but no production infrastructure implementing this as a standardized compliance and validation pipeline exists.
candidates.source_section: 3 How We Got Here: The Path to a Tool AI World in 2035

candidates.name: Focused Research Organizations (FROs)
candidates.source_quote: I think of them as a critical mass of the right people multiplied by a critical mass of time and support to build a very well-defined thing that the market would not support you building as a traditional for-profit startup, right? So in some ways you can think of them as sort of like nonprofit deep tech startups.
candidates.source_quote_context: Early discussion of what FROs are and how they differ from traditional organizations
candidates.speaker: Adam Marblestone
candidates.one_liner: Nonprofit startup-like entities that assemble a focused, interdisciplinary team to build a specific piece of scientific infrastructure that neither academia nor the private sector would otherwise produce.
candidates.mechanism: A parent nonprofit (Convergent Research) houses each FRO as a subsidiary LLC, providing back-office support. A small founding team handpicks hires for both technical skill and mission alignment, then operates with startup-like unity of purpose for roughly five years to build a well-defined deliverable—often an open-source dataset, tool, or platform. Unlike academic labs, all contributors converge on the same artifact rather than pursuing individual research questions.
candidates.exists_today: Convergent Research has launched several FROs including ones in connectomics, single-cell proteomics, and interactive theorem proving (Lean). A handful exist as of the recording, with the oldest approximately three years old.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Adam Marblestone | Solving Science’s Biggest Gaps.md

candidates.name: Lean FRO (interactive theorem proving infrastructure for mathematics and AI)
candidates.source_quote: Instead of writing down their mathematical proof on a piece of paper, they write it in this programming language, which is Lean. And then what Lean can also do in addition to suggesting next steps and so on and resolving parts of the proof, is it can actually just say, do your conclusions actually follow from your assumptions? Yes, you are right. Your proof is correct of the thing that you claim to be proving.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of specific FROs that have launched, highlighting the Lean FRO as an unexpected but important example
candidates.speaker: Adam Marblestone
candidates.one_liner: A focused research organization building software infrastructure around the Lean proof assistant, enabling automated verification of mathematical proofs and serving as a closed-loop training environment for AI systems.
candidates.mechanism: Mathematicians write proofs in the Lean programming language rather than on paper; the system can automatically verify whether conclusions follow from axioms. This creates a closed feedback loop analogous to a game engine (like Go or chess) where an AI can receive automatic reinforcement signals for correct proofs without human judges, potentially enabling AI to generate and verify novel mathematical proofs at scale. The FRO provides the software engineering capacity that mathematicians themselves lack.
candidates.exists_today: The Lean proof assistant language exists and is used by some mathematicians and AI researchers. DeepMind and others have used Lean-like environments for AI math research. The FRO to build out the broader infrastructure is the new organizational component.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Adam Marblestone | Solving Science’s Biggest Gaps.md

candidates.name: Bio-templated microchips via implosion fabrication
candidates.source_quote: Implosion fabrication is the opposite of expansion microscopy. It means you pattern materials into a hydrogel and then you shrink it, but it can shrink by a factor of more than 10 along each axis. And if you shrink something besides the wavelength of light down, you'd also get down to these single digit nanometer features.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of nanotechnology progress and what the field needs, specifically around positional chemistry and chip fabrication
candidates.speaker: Adam Marblestone
candidates.one_liner: A fabrication technique that patterns materials (potentially DNA origami or other biological scaffolds) into a hydrogel at optical resolution and then shrinks the hydrogel by 10x or more to achieve single-digit nanometer feature sizes for chip-like structures.
candidates.mechanism: Biological or chemical components are positioned within a swellable hydrogel using light-based patterning at resolutions accessible to conventional optics. The hydrogel is then chemically shrunk by a factor greater than 10 in each linear dimension, compressing the patterned features to nanometer scales that approach the precision needed for positional chemistry and chip fabrication. DNA origami provides a programmable scaffold at the ~2 nm scale that can serve as a starting template.
candidates.exists_today: Expansion microscopy (the reverse process) is widely used in neuroscience labs. Implosion fabrication has been demonstrated as a research technique at MIT. DNA origami is a mature research tool. Full integration into a chip fabrication pipeline does not yet exist.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Adam Marblestone | Solving Science’s Biggest Gaps.md

candidates.name: Vagus nerve microbiome characterization study
candidates.source_quote: One study I'm especially excited about involves collecting tissue from the vagus nerve, which connects the body and brain. It's responsible for some of the most important signaling between them. These samples come from people who, sadly, experience trauma and pass away in hospitals. As soon as that happens, surgeons can collect and preserve parts of the vagus nerve. We're now running the first-ever study characterizing the microbes — viruses, bacteria, and others — that might actually be living in that nerve.
candidates.source_quote_context: Amy describing PolyBio's tissue collection pipeline, roughly mid-interview around the tissue banking discussion
candidates.speaker: Amy Proal
candidates.one_liner: A first-of-its-kind study collecting and analyzing vagus nerve tissue from recently deceased trauma patients to characterize what viruses and bacteria reside in that nerve.
candidates.mechanism: Surgeons at partner hospitals collect vagus nerve tissue from trauma patients immediately after death and preserve it in solution. The tissue is then analyzed using metagenomic or similar techniques to identify microbial residents. Results are compared against other tissue and blood samples to understand what pathogens inhabit this critical brain-body signaling pathway.
candidates.exists_today: PolyBio states it is actively running this study; no prior published characterization of the living human vagus nerve microbiome exists at scale.

candidates.name: Extracellular vesicle-based blood diagnostics for tissue-resident infections
candidates.source_quote: Some groups use microfluidics to isolate extracellular vesicles in blood that might contain one or two pieces of a virus hiding deep in tissue. If you have the right tech, you can extract that signal. But these technologies are scattered across different labs, so we work to unite them — designing studies, for example in long COVID, where we collect both tissue and blood, then compare which diagnostic tests best reflect the infection in tissue.
candidates.source_quote_context: Amy explaining the diagnostic translation pipeline after describing tissue banking, in the section on moving from discovery to clinical tools
candidates.speaker: Amy Proal
candidates.one_liner: A validation framework pairing tissue biopsies with microfluidic blood assays that isolate extracellular vesicles carrying viral fragments, to develop accessible blood-based diagnostics for deep-tissue infections.
candidates.mechanism: Microfluidic platforms isolate extracellular vesicles circulating in blood; these vesicles can carry trace viral material shed from infected tissues. By simultaneously collecting matched tissue and blood samples from the same patients (e.g., long COVID cohorts), researchers can validate whether vesicle-based blood signals accurately reflect what is found in tissue, creating a calibrated diagnostic test that doesn't require biopsy.
candidates.exists_today: Microfluidic extracellular vesicle isolation exists in research settings; the specific cross-validation framework pairing it with tissue biopsy for persistent infection diagnosis is at early/prototype stage, not clinically deployed.

candidates.name: Multiplicity.ai
candidates.source_quote: It's called Multiplicity.ai. You can just ask a question and get answers from many AI systems at once and then see a synthesis of those, whether it's a table or a summary about what they agreed and disagreed on.
candidates.source_quote_context: Andrew describing products he has built, around timestamp 28:59
candidates.speaker: Andrew Critch
candidates.one_liner: A tool that queries multiple AI systems simultaneously and synthesizes their agreements and disagreements into a unified summary or table.
candidates.mechanism: A user submits a single question; the system routes it to multiple frontier LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) in parallel. A separate AI layer then compares and contrasts the responses, identifying points of agreement and disagreement, and presents the synthesis as a table or narrative summary. The goal is to reduce single-model bias on high-stakes questions.
candidates.exists_today: The product is live at Multiplicity.ai according to the speaker; it originated as a feature inside NotADoctor.ai before being spun out.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Andrew Critch | What AGI might look like in practice.md

candidates.name: NotADoctor.ai medical record serialization and RCT search
candidates.source_quote: It'll also help you collect your medical records very quickly from US health institutions—in about five minutes. I think 27,000 institutions you can collect through the app, and then it'll serialize your health record in a timeline that's both easier for you to read and easier for an LLM to read.
candidates.source_quote_context: Andrew describing his healthcare product, around timestamp 27:40
candidates.speaker: Andrew Critch
candidates.one_liner: A platform that aggregates a patient's medical records from thousands of US institutions, serializes them into an LLM-readable timeline, and cross-references them against randomized controlled trials relevant to the patient's conditions.
candidates.mechanism: Users authenticate against up to 27,000 US health institutions via the app, which pulls their records and restructures them into a chronological timeline formatted for both human readability and LLM ingestion. A search layer then matches the patient's conditions against a database of randomized controlled trials, surfacing relevant evidence. A multi-agent research feature (later spun into Multiplicity.ai) was developed to handle complex queries that single models handled poorly.
candidates.exists_today: Live product at NotADoctor.ai according to the speaker.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Andrew Critch | What AGI might look like in practice.md

candidates.name: AI-mediated conflict resolution tool (retorsion/disgorgement mediator)
candidates.source_quote: You could write a mediation tool that's like, 'Hey, we have a problem. Let's talk to this mediator.' And it'll try and get us the win-win. And if that fails, it'll try and get us the restoration. And if that fails, it'll try and get us the disgorgement.
candidates.source_quote_context: Andrew responding to a question about coordination challenges in de-escalatory self-defense, around timestamp 58:17
candidates.speaker: Andrew Critch
candidates.one_liner: A structured AI mediator that walks disputing parties through a prioritized sequence—win-win trade, then restoration, then disgorgement—before any punitive action is considered.
candidates.mechanism: The tool takes a described dispute and first attempts to surface a mutually beneficial trade between parties. If that fails, it seeks restoration of the original state. If restoration is refused, it facilitates disgorgement—eliminating the ill-gotten benefit without inflicting additional harm—and optionally a minimal retorsion sufficient to deter repetition. The explicit sequencing is meant to prevent escalation to revenge-level responses.
candidates.exists_today: No known implementation; described as a hypothetical product concept during the conversation.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Andrew Critch | What AGI might look like in practice.md

candidates.name: LitQA3 (high-recall literature evaluation benchmark)
candidates.source_quote: We're building another one right now which we're calling internally LitQA3, and this one is what I would call high-recall tasks. Right now, agents are really good at precision. Humanity's Last Exam is a very precision-level task: go find this one fact. We're trying to build evals that are what I would call recall tasks, like 'find every paper that studied X, do a meta-analysis to find out if X is true or false, and then give me statistics on whether that's true or not.'
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of benchmark limitations and Future House's evaluation work, mid-interview
candidates.speaker: Andrew White
candidates.one_liner: A benchmark that tests AI agents on high-recall scientific literature tasks—finding all relevant papers on a topic and synthesizing them into a meta-analysis—rather than single-fact retrieval.
candidates.mechanism: The benchmark poses tasks requiring an agent to locate every paper studying a given phenomenon, perform a meta-analysis across them, and return statistics on whether the phenomenon is supported. This contrasts with precision-style benchmarks (like Humanity's Last Exam) that ask for a single correct answer. The design targets a known weakness of current agents: integrating large bodies of evidence rather than retrieving isolated facts.
candidates.exists_today: Future House has a prior benchmark called Bioinformatics Benchmark (frontier LLMs score ~20%). LitQA3 is described as under active development ('we're building another one right now').
candidates.source_file: podcast/Andrew White | Building an AI Scientist to Automate Discovery.md

candidates.name: AI-driven drug repurposing pipeline (AMD/Ripasudil discovery workflow)
candidates.source_quote: We asked our system to come up with as many ideas as possible. It hypothesized about a lot of ideas about how this disease could be treated and then it used things like Owl to see if anybody had tried this before... And then based on these ideas that it thought could be good, what are experiments we could do in our lab? So then we did those experiments, then we provided the raw data to Finch, our data analysis agent... And then it proposed specific compounds to try to treat this in the cell model.
candidates.source_quote_context: Description of the dry AMD / Ripasudil discovery project, roughly mid-interview
candidates.speaker: Andrew White
candidates.one_liner: A multi-agent pipeline that takes a disease target as input and autonomously generates mechanistic hypotheses, checks prior art, designs wet-lab experiments, analyzes results, and proposes repurposed drug candidates—demonstrated end-to-end in ~3 weeks for dry AMD.
candidates.mechanism: The pipeline chains several specialized agents: a hypothesis-generation agent proposes mechanistic ideas; Owl searches clinical trials, patents, and literature for prior attempts; a wet-lab team executes agent-specified experiments; Finch (a data-analysis agent) builds and runs Jupyter notebooks on raw experimental data; and the system iterates to propose specific compounds. The AMD run identified Ripasudil (an existing glaucoma drug) as a candidate that accelerates macrophage debris clearance in the eye.
candidates.exists_today: A working prototype was used to produce a published paper on dry AMD/Ripasudil. The individual agents (Crow, Owl, Finch) are available via Future House's open API, but the fully automated end-to-end pipeline is not yet a packaged product.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Andrew White | Building an AI Scientist to Automate Discovery.md

candidates.name: Publishing for Machines (machine-readable scientific publishing framework)
candidates.source_quote: In my essay, I'm arguing that we need to start thinking about the consumers and producers of science as machines because we're reaching the point where human beings are not going to be able to comprehend all the information there... We need to start changing how we represent science... We need to have slimmer papers... the curation has to be separate... peer review which is the debate of science... that part of peer review is very important, but it shouldn't be hidden.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of scientific publishing reform, late in the interview
candidates.speaker: Andrew White
candidates.one_liner: A proposed redesign of scientific publishing that separates gatekeeping peer review from scientific debate, reduces paper size, eliminates prestige-based journal selection, minimizes latency, and structures outputs for machine ingestion rather than human readers.
candidates.mechanism: The framework has several components: (1) drastically reduced latency from project completion to public availability; (2) machine-readable formats replacing PDFs and paywalled corpora; (3) slimmer atomic publication units focused on single discoveries rather than multi-year projects; (4) separation of peer review into distinct functions—spam/fraud filtering vs. open scientific debate—with the debate portion made public rather than anonymous; and (5) removal of artificial scarcity/prestige signaling from the submission process. The underlying argument is that AI systems will soon be both the primary producers and consumers of scientific literature, making current human-centric formats obsolete.
candidates.exists_today: Preprint servers (arXiv, bioRxiv) address latency partially. Open-access mandates address paywalls partially. Post-publication peer review platforms (PubPeer, eLife's new model) address some debate-separation. White's synthesis into a unified 'publishing for machines' framework exists only as a draft essay.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Andrew White | Building an AI Scientist to Automate Discovery.md

candidates.name: Aviary
candidates.source_quote: We have this called Aviary, which is like a way to put together scientific agents. You can use our platform to do precedent search.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of open-source tools for early career scientists getting started in AI for science, near the end of the conversation
candidates.speaker: Andrew
candidates.one_liner: A scaffolding framework for composing and running scientific AI agents built by Future House.
candidates.mechanism: Aviary provides a structured way to combine large language models with tools to create scientific agents. It is part of a broader platform that includes capabilities like precedent search and is accessible via API. It is documented in a cookbook alongside other Future House tools like PaperQA.
candidates.exists_today: Exists as a released open-source project from Future House, accessible at futurehouse.org with documentation and API access, though adoption and scale are limited.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Andrew White | Building an AI Scientist to Automate Discovery.md

candidates.name: Loyal AI Assistance (Fiduciary AI Assistance)
candidates.source_quote: One of the things that came out of the augmented intelligence summit was fiduciary AI assistance. I have been calling them loyal AI assistance. There is a loyal AI system that doesn't have selfish interests and works to advance your goals and interests.
candidates.source_quote_context: Anthony Aguirre's response to the 'eucatastrophe' thought experiment near the end of the podcast
candidates.speaker: Anthony Aguirre
candidates.one_liner: A personal AI system explicitly designed to be loyal to the individual user's goals rather than to platform or advertiser interests, contrasted with current assistants like Siri or Alexa.
candidates.mechanism: The system would know the user deeply enough to assist rather than manipulate, with the user remaining in control. It would have no selfish or third-party interests baked in, functioning more like a fiduciary than a product. Some instances could assist with complex scientific problems while others help navigate everyday information dynamics.
candidates.exists_today: Current voice assistants (Siri, Alexa) and LLM-based assistants exist but are designed around platform interests; the 'fiduciary AI' framing was discussed at an augmented intelligence summit as a conceptual proposal without widespread implementation.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Anthony Aguirre & Anna Yelizarova | On Worldbuilding.md

candidates.name: Windfall Clause
candidates.source_quote: One paper that was interesting out of FHI was the Windfall Clause. This was an agreement where all these companies were building AGI. They agreed beforehand that if they build AI then a certain percentage of their money is reallocated into a trust.
candidates.source_quote_context: Anna Yelizarova's response to the 'eucatastrophe' thought experiment near the end of the podcast
candidates.speaker: Anna Yelizarova (citing FHI paper)
candidates.one_liner: A pre-committed contractual agreement among AGI-developing companies to redirect a percentage of windfall profits into a redistributive trust if they successfully build AGI.
candidates.mechanism: Companies developing AGI would sign on to the clause before achieving AGI, committing a defined share of extraordinary profits to a trust fund. This mechanism is designed to prevent extreme concentration of AGI-generated wealth and ensure broader societal benefit from the technology.
candidates.exists_today: Proposed in a Future of Humanity Institute paper; no major AI companies have formally adopted it, though it has been discussed in AI governance circles.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Anthony Aguirre & Anna Yelizarova | On Worldbuilding.md

candidates.name: Large-scale AI-mediated deliberation system
candidates.source_quote: With language models, we have the capability for a thousand people to have a conversation with another thousand people in real time. That's something we've never had the possibility for before, and we can now do it. I don't think we're quite doing it yet, but I suspect we will. What does that look like? That enables us to do things we could never do before—have 100,000 people come to a negotiated agreement on something in a real way.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of what excites the speaker about Tool AI futures, roughly two-thirds through the conversation
candidates.speaker: Anthony (last name not given)
candidates.one_liner: A system using language models to facilitate real-time structured deliberation and negotiated agreement among thousands or hundreds of thousands of people simultaneously.
candidates.mechanism: Language models mediate conversations between large groups of people in real time, aggregating and structuring preferences in ways that crowd dynamics alone cannot. Unlike voting (one bit of information every few years) or online shouting matches, the system would allow genuine back-and-forth negotiation at scale. The speaker envisions it as a tool-based complement to elected representation, not a replacement.
candidates.exists_today: Partial implementations exist in projects like Polis (used in Taiwan's vTaiwan process) and various AI-assisted deliberation experiments, but nothing operating at the scale or real-time negotiation depth described.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Anthony Aguirre | Tools or Agents? Choosing Our AI Future.md

candidates.name: Epistemic stack
candidates.source_quote: There is no reason why, when reading a newspaper article about something, you shouldn't be able to trace back: where did that quote come from, or where did this piece of information come from? How do I know whether to trust this?... We should be able to have a stack we can follow all the way from the high level back down to the raw ingredients, and then figure out how much we trust each of those steps.
candidates.source_quote_context: Answer to the final question about concrete shovel-ready Tool AI ideas, near the end of the conversation
candidates.speaker: Anthony (last name not given)
candidates.one_liner: A citation and provenance system for all information—from newspaper articles to social media claims—that lets users trace any assertion back to its raw data sources, with trust scores based on historical accuracy of each link in the chain.
candidates.mechanism: Every piece of information carries machine-readable provenance metadata linking it to its source, analogous to academic citations but applied universally. AI tools help users traverse this chain from a high-level claim down to raw data, which could be cryptographically signed by hardware secure enclaves and registered on a blockchain. Each node in the chain (person, outlet, inference step) accumulates a reliability record based on past accuracy, allowing users to assess how much to trust any given claim.
candidates.exists_today: Partial implementations exist in academic citation graphs, fact-checking overlays (e.g., Community Notes), and some blockchain-based content provenance projects (e.g., C2PA standard for media). No unified system spans from raw sensor data through inference to published claims with per-node trust scoring.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Anthony Aguirre | Tools or Agents? Choosing Our AI Future.md

candidates.name: Protein-based nanomachines for in vivo tissue repair and cleanup
candidates.source_quote: One of the things that we're very interested in now, which I think was in Eric's talk 20 years ago, is designing nanomachines that can circulate and clean up stuff that shouldn't be there, repair broken tissue, and so forth. And because we can design these new catalytic sites, we can use fuel molecules that nature never thought of. For example, it could be something that's in your diet, like there could be some type of food or food additive that actually when you eat it, it goes into your circulation through your body.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of molecular machines as the next industrial revolution, mid-interview
candidates.speaker: David Baker
candidates.one_liner: Designed protein nanomachines that circulate in the body, powered by dietary fuel molecules, to repair tissue and clear pathological material such as amyloid fibrils.
candidates.mechanism: The machines combine three engineered protein capabilities: target binding, conformational change (to transduce energy into motion), and catalysis (to hydrolyze a fuel molecule). A dietary compound—chosen specifically so it is not ubiquitous in food, allowing on/off control—enters circulation after ingestion and powers the cyclical mechanical action of the protein machine. The machine can then perform tasks such as disaggregating amyloid fibrils or clearing cellular debris outside cells, where no natural quality-control machinery exists.
candidates.exists_today: Baker Lab has prototype machines powered by chemical fuels and by light; natural molecular motors (myosin, kinesin) are well-characterized but not de novo designed. No dietary-fueled, therapeutically functional de novo protein nanomachine has been demonstrated in vivo.
candidates.source_file: podcast/David Baker | Using AI for Science to Solve Humanity's Biggest Problems.md

candidates.name: De novo designed universal flu vaccines (Neil King / Baker Lab platform)
candidates.source_quote: My colleague Neil King actually made the first de novo design medicine, a vaccine, and he's working to make universal flu vaccines and in general vaccines that could protect against as-yet-unknown viruses.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of health applications of protein design, late in the interview
candidates.speaker: David Baker (describing Neil King's work)
candidates.one_liner: Computationally designed protein nanoparticle scaffolds that present conserved viral epitopes to generate broad, cross-strain protective immunity against influenza and future unknown viruses.
candidates.mechanism: De novo protein design is used to create self-assembling nanoparticle scaffolds that display conserved antigenic regions of influenza (and potentially other viruses) in precise geometric arrangements. Because the scaffold and antigen presentation geometry are designed from first principles rather than derived from attenuated virus, the platform can be rapidly retargeted to novel pathogens. The goal is to elicit antibodies against epitopes shared across many strains, providing universal rather than strain-specific protection.
candidates.exists_today: Neil King's lab has published de novo designed nanoparticle vaccines that entered clinical trials (e.g., ferritin-based and two-component nanoparticle flu vaccine candidates). A fully universal flu vaccine is not yet approved or deployed at scale.
candidates.source_file: podcast/David Baker | Using AI for Science to Solve Humanity's Biggest Problems.md

candidates.name: Universal Constructor
candidates.source_quote: I think it will be important, and after the universal constructor is first built, it can then build exponentially more. The human role in production will no longer ever involve unpleasant physical work. Toil will be completely ended by the invention of the universal constructor.
candidates.source_quote_context: Near the end of the podcast, in response to the 'eucatastrophe' question from Beatrice Erkers
candidates.speaker: David Deutsch
candidates.one_liner: A physical machine that can be programmed to construct any physically possible object or perform any physically possible transformation, analogous to a universal computer but for matter.
candidates.mechanism: A universal constructor must be perfectly obedient to its program and capable of being reprogrammed to perform any task not prohibited by the laws of physics. Like a universal computer generalizes computation, a universal constructor generalizes physical fabrication. Deutsch envisions it as something like a computer paired with a robot, where humans provide knowledge and programming rather than physical labor, with sophisticated AI-like interfaces (analogous to ChatGPT for code) handling the translation of intent into constructor instructions.
candidates.exists_today: Constructor theory as a research program exists (developed by Deutsch and Chiara Marletto). Modern CNC machines, 3D printers, and robotic manufacturing are narrow constructors. No general-purpose universal constructor has been built; Deutsch notes 'we do not know how to make a real universal constructor yet.'
candidates.source_file: podcast/David Deutsch | On Beauty, Knowledge, and Progress.md

candidates.name: Liberal/Popperian AGI Education Framework
candidates.source_quote: If AGI were invented tomorrow, it would indeed be the right thing to do to educate the newly programmed AGI as closely as possible to the way our society educates children... to do it for AGI is not impossible either.
candidates.source_quote_context: Early in the podcast during discussion of AI alignment and Taking Children Seriously, in response to Allison Duettmann's question about applying TCS to AI
candidates.speaker: David Deutsch
candidates.one_liner: A proposed approach to AGI alignment modeled on liberal Enlightenment child-rearing principles rather than hard-coded constraints or enforced behavioral rules, treating AGI as a creative entity that must develop values through conjecture and criticism rather than obedience.
candidates.mechanism: Rather than building alignment into hardware or enforcing behavioral constraints (which Deutsch calls 'attempted enslavement'), an AGI would be raised in an environment mirroring how liberal societies socialize children—through exposure to norms, freedom to conjecture, and error-correction via criticism. The analogy draws on how Western institutions solved the problem of human violence not through coercion but through cultural evolution of consent-based governance. The key distinction is that this applies only to true AGI (creative, general intelligence), not to narrow AI systems where obedience-enforcement is appropriate and desirable.
candidates.exists_today: Taking Children Seriously exists as a philosophy. Constitutional AI (Anthropic) and RLHF represent current alignment approaches, which Deutsch would characterize as the opposite of his proposal. No AGI exists to apply this to; the framework remains theoretical.
candidates.source_file: podcast/David Deutsch | On Beauty, Knowledge, and Progress.md

candidates.name: LLM Historical Forecasting Benchmark
candidates.source_quote: I'm collaborating with Alec Bradford and Nick Levine: training LLMs on only pre-1930 data, then testing whether they can 'forecast' the 1930s–40s. It's hard — leakage, framing questions, calibration — but promising.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of forecasting as a field, near the end of the interview around the forecasting topic section
candidates.speaker: David Duvenaud
candidates.one_liner: A system for evaluating long-term AI forecasting ability by training LLMs on pre-1930 data and testing whether they can accurately predict known historical outcomes from the 1930s–40s.
candidates.mechanism: LLMs are trained exclusively on historical data up to a cutoff date (pre-1930), then asked to forecast events that occurred afterward (1930s–40s), where ground truth is known. This creates a controlled benchmark for measuring long-term forecasting calibration. Key challenges include preventing data leakage, properly framing questions, and measuring calibration against known outcomes.
candidates.exists_today: The collaboration between Duvenaud, Alec Bradford, and Nick Levine is described as ongoing work; no published results mentioned. General LLM benchmarking exists widely, but this specific historical forecasting evaluation methodology does not appear to be deployed at scale.
candidates.source_file: podcast/David Duvenaud | Exploring the Cruxes and Possibilities of Post AGI Futures.md

candidates.name: Futarchy
candidates.source_quote: Robin's idea is: separate values from predictions. We'd vote on values — the government's utility function. Then use prediction markets to forecast which policies best achieve those values. Expert forecasters would be incentivized to get it right.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section on Robin Hanson's futarchy, prompted by interviewer question near timestamp ~51:26
candidates.speaker: Robin Hanson (described by David Duvenaud)
candidates.one_liner: A governance system where citizens vote on societal values/objectives, and prediction markets determine which policies are forecast to best achieve those values, replacing expert policy judgment with incentivized forecasting.
candidates.mechanism: The system splits governance into two layers: a democratic vote establishes the utility function (what outcomes society wants), and prediction markets are used to evaluate which candidate policies are most likely to achieve those outcomes. Forecasters are financially incentivized to make accurate predictions, theoretically producing better policy selection than expert committees or political deliberation. Robin Hanson has run small experiments, but adoption has stalled because leaders feel undermined when markets forecast their preferred policies will fail.
candidates.exists_today: Small internal corporate prediction markets have been tried (and largely abandoned). Robin Hanson has helped set up limited experiments. No government has implemented futarchy at scale. Prediction markets like Metaculus and Polymarket exist but are not integrated into formal policy selection.
candidates.source_file: podcast/David Duvenaud | Exploring the Cruxes and Possibilities of Post AGI Futures.md

candidates.name: Programmable synthetic molecular robots for chemical synthesis
candidates.source_quote: That is some of the work we focus on, which is making these first programmable, synthetic molecular robots that can do simple, chemical reactions. As that becomes more and more sophisticated, we will be able to build more and more complicated structures.
candidates.source_quote_context: Response to audience question about nanobots and atomic precision construction, near end of interview
candidates.speaker: David Leigh
candidates.one_liner: Synthetic molecular-scale robots that can be programmed to perform specific chemical reactions and sequentially build complex molecular structures.
candidates.mechanism: Drawing on biological analogies like polyketide synthase super-enzyme complexes that pass building blocks from active site to active site, these synthetic molecular robots are designed to perform discrete chemical operations in a programmable sequence. The machines exploit controlled Brownian motion (random thermal movement directionally biased by asymmetric energy input) rather than macroscopic engineering principles. Early prototypes perform simple reactions; increasing sophistication is expected to enable assembly of more complex molecular architectures.
candidates.exists_today: Early-stage prototypes exist in Leigh's lab and similar groups; biological analogues (ribosome, polyketide synthases) are well-characterized. No general-purpose synthetic molecular assembler has been demonstrated.
candidates.source_file: podcast/David Leigh | Exploring the possibilities of nanotechnology.md

candidates.name: Active smart fabric with autonomous environmental response
candidates.source_quote: Imagine my shirt being like a computer, and being able to respond to its environment, sense things, and develop protection. For instance, if it sensed viruses, it could put out antiviral bits on the surface or close the distance between the fibers to stop penetration. All of these sorts of things could happen autonomously through active materials.
candidates.source_quote_context: Leigh's recommendation to prospective researchers on promising application areas, mid-interview
candidates.speaker: David Leigh
candidates.one_liner: Textile materials embedded with molecular machines that autonomously sense environmental stimuli (e.g., pathogens) and alter surface chemistry or fiber geometry in response.
candidates.mechanism: Molecular machines incorporated into fabric fibers would use chemical, light, or electrical energy inputs to drive conformational changes—altering fiber spacing, surface chemistry, or displaying functional molecules (e.g., antivirals). The machines act as transducers between an environmental signal and a mechanical or chemical output, analogous to how biological molecular machines couple energy to directed motion. Because only surface-level quantities of material are needed, this is considered a near-term feasible application compared to bulk molecular manufacturing.
candidates.exists_today: Mechanically interlocked molecules (rotaxanes/catenanes) are already used in some phone screen coatings to improve mechanical properties. Stimuli-responsive polymers and shape-memory textiles exist but lack the molecular-machine-driven autonomous sensing-and-response capability described.
candidates.source_file: podcast/David Leigh | Exploring the possibilities of nanotechnology.md

candidates.name: Gene Drives for Wild Animal Suffering Reduction
candidates.source_quote: Gene drives cheat the laws of Mendelian inheritance, enabling the spread of beneficial genes in populations, offering a novel approach to address issues like vector-borne diseases.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section on Genetic Engineering Advancements in Addressing Animal Suffering, around timestamp 09:55
candidates.speaker: David Pearce
candidates.one_liner: Using gene drive technology to spread genes that reduce pain sensitivity or regulate fertility through wild animal populations to reduce suffering in nature.
candidates.mechanism: Gene drives override normal Mendelian inheritance so that a modified gene spreads through a population far faster than natural selection would allow. Applied to wild animals, this could propagate alleles that reduce pain sensitivity or otherwise lower suffering. The same mechanism already proposed for eliminating malaria-carrying mosquitoes would be repurposed for broader wildlife welfare goals.
candidates.exists_today: Gene drives have been demonstrated in laboratory settings (e.g., CRISPR-based drives in mosquitoes by Target Malaria). No deployment for wild animal welfare has occurred; it remains a research-stage proposal.
candidates.source_file: podcast/David Pearce | A Future without Suffering.md

candidates.name: Elective Cryonic Suspension at Peak Vitality ('Kyasia')
candidates.source_quote: Kyasia is more controversial, the idea that instead of waiting until you're, let's say, 95 and pretty decrepit, you could be suspended after being, yeah, retired, so to speak, but in optimal conditions.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section on Cryonics and Longevity Progress, around timestamp 28:39
candidates.speaker: David Pearce (attributed to Foresight Institute context)
candidates.one_liner: A protocol for voluntarily entering cryonic suspension while still healthy and vital, rather than waiting until near-death, to maximize revival prospects.
candidates.mechanism: Rather than using cryonics only as a last resort at end of life when the body is severely degraded, individuals would elect suspension at a younger, healthier age (e.g., mid-70s). The premise is that preservation quality is higher in a vital body, improving the odds that future technology can successfully revive and rejuvenate the individual. It requires both the cryonics infrastructure and a legal/social framework permitting elective suspension.
candidates.exists_today: Standard cryonics (post-legal-death suspension) exists through organizations like Alcor and Cryonics Institute. Elective suspension of healthy individuals is not legally permitted anywhere and has no operational implementation.
candidates.source_file: podcast/David Pearce | A Future without Suffering.md

candidates.name: Phenomenal Binding-Based Sentient AI Architecture
candidates.source_quote: I regard computers with existing architecture as cognitively crippled because they cannot solve the phenomenal binding problem, therefore they are non-sentient and they are never going to wake up.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section on Skepticism on the Conception of Superintelligence, around timestamp 37:35
candidates.speaker: David Pearce
candidates.one_liner: A proposed alternative AI architecture that solves the phenomenal binding problem, enabling genuine sentience rather than the 'digital zombie' behavior of classical computers.
candidates.mechanism: Pearce argues that classical digital computers process information in ways that cannot produce unified conscious experience because they cannot bind disparate neural/computational signals into a single phenomenal subject. A genuinely sentient AI would require a different physical substrate or architecture capable of phenomenal binding—possibly exploiting quantum coherence or other non-classical physics—so that the system has a unified point of view and can reflect on and manipulate its own mental states. Without this, he contends, no amount of scaling classical systems produces real superintelligence.
candidates.exists_today: No implementation exists. The binding problem itself remains unsolved in neuroscience. Some quantum mind theories (e.g., Penrose-Hameroff) gesture at related ideas but have no engineering instantiation.
candidates.source_file: podcast/David Pearce | A Future without Suffering.md

candidates.name: Aldehyde-Stabilized Cryopreservation
candidates.source_quote: The most promising technique I think that exists currently, the most promising brain preservation technique, is one called aldehyde-stabilized cryopreservation. So what it does is it combines an initial fixation step, which is when you introduce chemicals that sort of form a gel-like matrix inside a person's body and brain, before you do the vitrification and before you do the cooling.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of brain preservation techniques, approximately mid-interview when asked about the most promising method
candidates.speaker: Ariel Zeleznikow-Johnston
candidates.one_liner: A two-step brain preservation technique that chemically fixes neural tissue before vitrification to prevent shrinkage and preserve synaptic structure.
candidates.mechanism: Aldehyde chemicals are introduced first to form a gel-like matrix that locks all neural structures in place. This fixation step prevents the volume reduction (up to 50%) seen with vitrification alone, because the matrix resists the osmotic effects of cryoprotectants. The brain is then cooled and vitrified without ice formation or structural damage, leaving neurons and synapses traceable under electron microscopy.
candidates.exists_today: Exists as a laboratory technique; won the Brain Preservation Foundation's large mammal prize around 2018 after developers demonstrated near-perfect preservation of animal brains under electron microscopy. Not yet integrated into clinical or hospice settings for human use.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Dr Ariel Zeleznikow-Johnston | The Future Loves You.md

candidates.name: Integration of Brain Preservation into the Medical System
candidates.source_quote: The thing that I most think about and most would like to happen is to see the integration of brain preservation technologies into the medical system, where each individual who is approaching the end of their life can make a choice that I would like to be preserved when I reach a certain threshold of illness, when I am imminently dying... And that would look like integration of these brain preservation facilities into hospitals, into hospices.
candidates.source_quote_context: Near the end of the interview, in response to the 'eucatastrophe' question
candidates.speaker: Ariel Zeleznikow-Johnston
candidates.one_liner: A proposed clinical pathway allowing terminally ill patients to opt into brain preservation as a standard end-of-life option within hospitals and hospices.
candidates.mechanism: Patients approaching death would be offered brain preservation (e.g., aldehyde-stabilized cryopreservation) as a formal medical choice alongside palliative care, requiring consent frameworks, procedural integration with existing patient care workflows, and dedicated preservation facilities co-located with or linked to hospitals and hospices. The preserved brain would be stored with the expectation of future revival via whole brain emulation or nanotechnology.
candidates.exists_today: Private cryonics organizations (e.g., Alcor, Cryonics Institute) offer analogous services outside the mainstream medical system, but no hospital or hospice system has formally integrated brain preservation as a standard end-of-life option.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Dr Ariel Zeleznikow-Johnston | The Future Loves You.md

candidates.name: Brain Preservation Integration into Medical System
candidates.source_quote: The thing that I most think about and most would like to happen is to see the integration of brain preservation technologies into the medical system, where each individual who is approaching the end of their life can make a choice that I would like to be preserved when I reach a certain threshold of illness, when I am imminently dying, such that there is some realistic chance that at some point in the future, my preserved body or me can be revived.
candidates.source_quote_context: Speaker answering the 'eucatastrophe' question around timestamp 00:40:28
candidates.speaker: Ariel
candidates.one_liner: A country-scale system integrating brain preservation (cryonics-style) into hospitals and hospices as an elective end-of-life option, with long-term storage infrastructure.
candidates.mechanism: Individuals approaching death would opt in to brain preservation procedures performed at hospitals or hospices. Preserved bodies would be stored in dedicated warehouse facilities. The system would require shared political will to develop revival technologies alongside the preservation infrastructure. The speaker estimates ~$10,000 per procedure and a few hundred to a few thousand dollars per year in storage costs at country-wide scale.
candidates.exists_today: Private cryonics organizations (Alcor, Cryonics Institute) already offer brain and whole-body preservation, but these are niche, expensive, and entirely outside mainstream medical systems. No country has integrated such options into standard end-of-life healthcare pathways.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Dr Ariel Zeleznikow-Johnston | The Future Loves You.md

candidates.name: Imagination Annotated (book series)
candidates.source_quote: We're also starting a new book series with MIT Press where we're going to annotate other works of science fiction. So that's called Imagination Annotated. And the first volume will be Jules Verne's From the Earth to the Moon.
candidates.source_quote_context: Near the end of the conversation, after discussing Frankenbook, Ed Finn mentions a new forthcoming series
candidates.speaker: Ed Finn
candidates.one_liner: A MIT Press book series that annotates classic science fiction works with commentary from scientists, engineers, and other domain experts, following the model of the Frankenstein annotated edition.
candidates.mechanism: Each volume takes a canonical science fiction text and layers it with annotations from researchers and practitioners across relevant fields, connecting the speculative ideas in the fiction to contemporary science, ethics, and technology. The Frankenstein volume (Frankenbook) demonstrated the model: annotations appear alongside the original text, supplemented by short videos and online media at a companion website. The goal is to use the fiction as a scaffold for interdisciplinary dialogue about what the speculative ideas mean for the next era of science and society.
candidates.exists_today: The Frankenstein volume (Frankenbook) is fully published by MIT Press and available online at frankenbook.org with annotations and video. The Jules Verne volume is in development but not yet published.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Ed Finn | How Science Fiction Can Inspire Real-World Innovation.md

candidates.name: Project Hieroglyph
candidates.source_quote: Neal's line that I quote all the time is, 'A good science fiction story can save you hundreds of hours of PowerPoint presentations and meetings because it literally puts everybody on the same page.' So you can read a story about rocket ships by Jules Verne or Robert Heinlein or somebody like that and you can get this concept.
candidates.source_quote_context: Early in the conversation when Ed Finn explains the origin and concept of Project Hieroglyph
candidates.speaker: Ed Finn / Neal Stephenson
candidates.one_liner: An anthology and collaborative platform pairing science fiction writers with researchers and students to produce technically grounded, hopeful near-future stories intended to serve as inspirational 'hieroglyphs' — shared conceptual targets that can drive real innovation.
candidates.mechanism: Writers, researchers, and students interact on a shared platform to co-develop story concepts under loose guidelines (possible, plausible, preferable; no magical technologies, no easy apocalypse, no lone-hacker savior narratives). The resulting stories function as compressed cognitive simulations of futures that diverse stakeholders can inhabit, debate, and extend — creating shared vocabulary and aspirational goals across disciplinary silos. The anthology format then disseminates these hieroglyphs broadly.
candidates.exists_today: The Hieroglyph anthology was published (edited by Ed Finn and Kathryn Cramer). The companion website with writer-researcher-student discussions has since been deprecated. The Center for Science and the Imagination at ASU continues related projects.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Ed Finn | How Science Fiction Can Inspire Real-World Innovation.md

candidates.name: AI-powered blog aggregator with conversational interface
candidates.source_quote: Maybe it's like the OpenAI GPT mode - you could tell the AI to follow all your favorite blogs. Then you go for a walk, have your headphones on, and just ask 'Samantha' what's been going on in the blogs lately. Then she tells you, and you can ask questions and have a conversation about it.
candidates.source_quote_context: Near the end of the conversation, discussing how to keep up with the volume of progress-related writing online
candidates.speaker: Eli Dourado
candidates.one_liner: A conversational AI agent that monitors a user's subscribed blogs and newsletters, then delivers and discusses their content on demand via voice.
candidates.mechanism: The system would track a curated list of blogs and Substacks, ingest new content as it's published, and synthesize it for the user. The user interacts via voice (e.g., during a walk), asking the AI to summarize recent posts or drill into specific topics, with the AI able to answer follow-up questions conversationally based on the source material.
candidates.exists_today: Podcast apps and some Substack features offer text-to-speech for individual posts. AI assistants like ChatGPT can discuss content if manually pasted in, but no product currently combines automatic multi-source blog monitoring with a persistent, conversational, voice-first interface.

candidates.name: Privacy-Preserving Global Regulatory Markets for AI Verification
candidates.source_quote: Interesting papers have been published on creating global regulatory markets for AI that are privacy-preserving, allowing different actors to verify models based on agreed-upon agreements.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section on Positive AI Technologies, near the end of the transcript
candidates.speaker: Emilia Javorsky (summarizing published research)
candidates.one_liner: A proposed market-based regulatory framework where AI models can be verified by multiple actors using privacy-preserving methods against shared compliance agreements.
candidates.mechanism: Different actors (governments, civil society, companies) would participate in a global regulatory market where AI models are submitted for verification. Privacy-preserving techniques would allow auditors to check model properties against agreed-upon standards without exposing proprietary model internals. The market structure would create incentives for compliance and enable multi-stakeholder verification.
candidates.exists_today: Exists as academic papers and proposals; cryptographic techniques like zero-knowledge proofs exist that could underpin such a system, but no operational global regulatory market for AI verification has been deployed.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Emilia Javorsky | The Future of AI, Bioengineering, and Human Empathy.md

candidates.name: Bell Labs Systems Engineer Role
candidates.source_quote: A Bell Labs-flavored systems engineer has a place in almost all of them. If you say, 'Oh, our research doesn't need to be useful for 20 years,' that's fantastic; in that case, the markets that are interesting to your systems engineer really expand.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of Bell Labs management practices and how they could be applied to new science organizations
candidates.speaker: Eric Gilliam
candidates.one_liner: A dedicated role within new science organizations whose job is to survey both the applied/commercial side of operations and the basic research side, then broker connections between researchers and high-value unsolved problems.
candidates.mechanism: The systems engineer spends roughly half their time touring manufacturing operations or poring over budgets to identify high-value problems (with explicit market sizing), and the other half walking the research labs to understand who is working on what and who might be interested in which problems. When a match is found, they broker the connection and help justify research budgets by anchoring them to concrete problem value. This creates a 'long leash within a narrow fence' dynamic: researchers have freedom to pursue problems deeply, but the fence is drawn around commercially or practically significant areas.
candidates.exists_today: Bell Labs had this role historically; some modern research organizations have informal versions (e.g., program managers at DARPA/ARPA-E play a partial analog), but the specific institutionalized role as described is not standard in contemporary new science organizations or FROs.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Eric Gilliam | What history can teach us about doing better science.md

candidates.name: BBN-style Applied R&D Contractor (New BBNs)
candidates.source_quote: I would set up shop with the $100 million and I'd say, 'I want to wholly fund, wholly seed fund, BBNs or would-be BBNs that want to service some ambitious area of R&D.' Is it because an area of research needs a systems engineer, testbed technology, like a group to tie it all together and make it workable, expand the ambitions of the field, whatever it is? Or do you just want to service a field and you think it could be 10 times as productive if they had some group that serves a non-VC market?
candidates.source_quote_context: Eric Gilliam's answer to the hypothetical '$100 million to start a new organization' question, describing his preferred model
candidates.speaker: Eric Gilliam
candidates.one_liner: A new class of small, technically ambitious applied R&D firms that pursue an FRO-style technical vision funded through a mix of contracts and grants, serving research fields that lack testbed technology or systems integration capacity and are not addressable by VC.
candidates.mechanism: A BBN is seeded with a small amount of capital ($500K–$2M) and warm introductions to potential customers. It identifies a technically ambitious goal (e.g., real-time computing, autonomous vehicles) and funds itself by taking on contracts that happen to de-risk the core technology—even if the contract domain (e.g., hospital records digitization) is not the ultimate goal. Over time, by iterating on the technology through these contracts, the organization builds unique capability that positions it to execute on larger, more ambitious programs (e.g., ARPANET) when the opportunity arises. Three pillars: novelty-seeking technical ambition, a mix of contracts/grants as revenue, and a practical engineering orientation distinct from both academia and large defense contractors.
candidates.exists_today: The original BBN (Bolt, Beranek, and Newman) is the historical exemplar; CMU's robotics institute is a nonprofit analog. Some CROs and national labs partially overlap, but the specific combination of FRO-style vision, contract-funded de-risking, and small founding team is not a recognized organizational category today. Eric Gilliam is actively working with ARIA (UK) to instantiate this model.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Eric Gilliam | What history can teach us about doing better science.md

candidates.name: Focused Philanthropic Bet Modeled on Warren Weaver / Rockefeller Molecular Biology Program
candidates.source_quote: If I were going to do basic research with the $100 million, I would try to find some area that I thought $100 million over 10 years or something could go a long way with that kind of thinking... I would like you, Warren, and potential Warren Weavers, to come to me, and one of you will get these funds, and we're not going to have a bureaucratic foundation. It's going to be just you.
candidates.source_quote_context: Eric Gilliam's answer to the hypothetical '$100 million to start a new organization' question, describing the basic research variant of his preferred model
candidates.speaker: Eric Gilliam
candidates.one_liner: A lean philanthropic structure that concentrates ~80% of a science foundation's budget on a single under-funded interdisciplinary area identified by one empowered program officer, with the explicit plan to exit the area once mainstream funders adopt it.
candidates.mechanism: A single technically sophisticated program officer (the 'Warren Weaver') is given near-total discretion over a concentrated budget, supported by only one or two technical staffers. They identify a field at the intersection of two disciplines where tools from one can unlock the other, fund it heavily before it is recognized as important, and explicitly plan to redeploy capital once the field becomes mainstream (as Weaver did after Watson and Crick). The remaining ~20% of budget is used for exploratory side bets that may become the next concentrated bet. No grant committees or bureaucratic review processes.
candidates.exists_today: The original Rockefeller Foundation Natural Sciences Division under Warren Weaver (1932–1952) is the historical model. Some aspects exist in programs like the Open Philanthropy 'cause prioritization' approach or the Wellcome Trust's Sanger Institute bet, but the specific structure of a single empowered officer with near-total budget discretion and a planned exit strategy is not standard practice in contemporary science philanthropy.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Eric Gilliam | What history can teach us about doing better science.md

candidates.name: Viotopia
candidates.source_quote: One answer—it's not my idea, but something I'd love to think about—is this concept from Will MacAskill of a 'viotopia' (via meaning 'on the way'). The thought is that this is a state of the world where, if you enter it, you're very likely for the rest of the future to go really well. It's the checkpoint we want to reach.
candidates.source_quote_context: Near the end of the conversation, when Fin is asked about half-baked ideas he is currently thinking about
candidates.speaker: Will MacAskill (discussed by Fin Moorhouse)
candidates.one_liner: A self-sustaining civilizational checkpoint state that, once reached, makes very good long-run futures highly probable.
candidates.mechanism: The viotopia is conceived as a stable attractor state for civilization rather than a final utopian endpoint. It must be self-sustaining, work at scale, include procedures for deliberation, and maintain option value and diversity. Reaching it is the actionable near-term target because it does not require specifying the full content of a great future, only the conditions that make such futures likely.
candidates.exists_today: No implementation exists; it is a philosophical/strategic concept introduced in the Forethought 'Better Futures' series. Related ideas appear in work on 'long reflection' and stable governance frameworks.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Fin Moorhouse | Why We Need to Aim Higher Than Survival.md

candidates.name: Moral Trade
candidates.source_quote: Let's say you really care that people abstain from eating meat, and I really care about people reducing their carbon footprint. Maybe it's not much of a cost for me to eliminate meat from my diet, and it's not much of a cost for you to offset your emissions. Then we have an opportunity for a deal where I eat less meat and you reduce your carbon footprint... if you scale it up to the level of a civilization, there are huge opportunities.
candidates.source_quote_context: Mid-conversation section on positive-sum mechanisms for reaching better futures, prompted by discussion of the 'Archipelago' concept
candidates.speaker: Fin Moorhouse (crediting Toby Ord as originator)
candidates.one_liner: A mechanism by which people or groups with different moral priorities swap concessions so that each gets more of what they care about than unilateral action would yield.
