candidates.mechanism: Analogous to economic trade but applied to altruistic or ethical preferences: parties identify where their moral priorities are cheap for the other side to accommodate, then negotiate exchanges. At civilizational scale this could allow diverse moral communities to each achieve far more of their valued outcomes than competition or majority-rule would permit, without requiring any single moral view to dominate.
candidates.exists_today: Toby Ord named and theorized the concept academically; small-scale informal versions occur in activist coalition bargaining, but no institutional infrastructure for large-scale moral trade exists.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Fin Moorhouse | Why We Need to Aim Higher Than Survival.md

candidates.name: Provably Safe AGI via Formal Verification
candidates.source_quote: we can do something with mathematical proofs where we can potentially prove that certain small systems are safe, and then perhaps expand on those systems until we get something that's we can prove the safety properties of larger and larger systems.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of undervalued AI safety approaches, referencing the Steve Omohundro podcast episode on 'provably safe AGI'
candidates.speaker: Gus Docker (referencing Steve Omohundro)
candidates.one_liner: A formal verification approach to AI safety that proves safety properties of small systems and compositionally scales those proofs to larger systems.
candidates.mechanism: Start by mathematically proving safety properties of small, tractable AI systems. Then expand those verified systems incrementally, extending the proofs to cover larger and more capable systems. AI itself may be used to assist in generating the complex proofs required. The concern is whether proof-generation capabilities can keep pace with general AI capability growth.
candidates.exists_today: Formal verification exists in software engineering and hardware; Steve Omohundro and others have written about applying it to AI. No large-scale AI system has been proven safe in this way; it remains a research direction.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Gus Docker | Beyond Survival: Envisioning A Technologically Enhanced Utopia.md

candidates.name: Meditation-State Detection Model
candidates.source_quote: there's a project ongoing right now trying to train a model on data from very advanced meditators reaching specific states of meditation that are supposed to be very blissful. What you can do there is to try to see if you can train a model to detect that state in inexperienced meditators. And also you can try to cross-reference what the signature of the state looks like for one advanced meditator and then check to see that all of the advanced meditators are actually reaching the state.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of technologies relevant to positive futures and exploring conscious states, in the worldbuilding/2050 section of the interview
candidates.speaker: Gus Docker
candidates.one_liner: A narrow AI model trained on neurological data from expert meditators to detect and validate specific high-valence meditative states in novice practitioners.
candidates.mechanism: Collect neural or physiological data from advanced meditators who reliably reach specific high-bliss states. Train a model to recognize the signature of that state. Apply the model to inexperienced meditators to guide them toward the state, and cross-validate across multiple advanced meditators to confirm the state signature is consistent and real rather than idiosyncratic.
candidates.exists_today: EEG-based neurofeedback for meditation guidance exists commercially (e.g., Muse headband). Research labs have studied neural correlates of meditative states. A model specifically trained to detect and cross-validate advanced bliss states across practitioners at this level of rigor does not appear to be widely deployed.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Gus Docker | Beyond Survival: Envisioning A Technologically Enhanced Utopia.md

candidates.name: Closed-loop ultrasound brain-state readout and mood modulation system
candidates.source_quote: A collaboration among Forrest Neurotech, the NHS, and the University of Plymouth: can we read out brain state (via blood-flow changes akin to Doppler) and target specific circuit elements to perturb mood—all non-invasively? Neurons have mechanosensitive ion channels—ultrasound can 'squidge' them and induce firing reversibly, without damage. This is in a clinical trial.
candidates.source_quote_context: Jacques describing concrete funded projects under the Precision Neurotechnologies program
candidates.speaker: Jacques Carolan
candidates.one_liner: A non-invasive closed-loop system that uses ultrasound Doppler to read brain state and then stimulates mechanosensitive ion channels in targeted circuits to modulate mood.
candidates.mechanism: The system reads cerebral blood-flow changes via Doppler ultrasound as a proxy for brain state. It then delivers focused ultrasound pulses to specific circuit elements, mechanically activating ion channels in neurons to induce or suppress firing reversibly. The closed-loop design means readout informs stimulation parameters in real time.
candidates.exists_today: Currently in a clinical trial run by Forrest Neurotech, the NHS, and the University of Plymouth; focused ultrasound neuromodulation exists in research but closed-loop mood-targeting at this specificity is not yet standard care.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Jacques Carolan | The future of brain health.md

candidates.name: Closed-loop gene therapy for seizure suppression via activity-sensing potassium-channel upregulation
candidates.source_quote: A team at UCL is developing closed-loop gene therapies initially for epilepsy. The therapy senses increased activity (e.g., a seizure) and upregulates potassium channels—putting the brakes on neurons—to stop the seizure. We're funding them to expand access in different brain regions, explore ultrasound activation, and apply to other conditions.
candidates.source_quote_context: Jacques listing funded Precision Neurotechnologies projects
candidates.speaker: Jacques Carolan
candidates.one_liner: A gene therapy that autonomously senses pathological neural activity and upregulates inhibitory potassium channels in situ to abort seizures without external hardware.
candidates.mechanism: Engineered genetic constructs are delivered to neurons; a sensing element detects elevated electrical activity characteristic of seizure onset and triggers expression or activation of potassium channels, hyperpolarizing the neurons and terminating the seizure. ARIA funding extends this to additional brain regions, explores ultrasound as an external activation trigger, and investigates application to conditions beyond epilepsy.
candidates.exists_today: UCL team has a working prototype; optogenetic and chemogenetic closed-loop seizure suppression exists in animal models; human closed-loop gene therapy for epilepsy is not yet approved or widely deployed.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Jacques Carolan | The future of brain health.md

candidates.name: Biohybrid living DBS electrode (neuron-based implant interface)
candidates.source_quote: Implanted electrodes are mechanically mismatched to soft brain tissue, leading to scarring and signal issues, and they don't provide cell-type access. If you could grow neurons to serve as an interface, you might achieve better circuit specificity. We're funding teams to explore something akin to a living DBS electrode.
candidates.source_quote_context: Jacques listing funded Precision Neurotechnologies projects
candidates.speaker: Jacques Carolan
candidates.one_liner: An implantable interface made of living neurons rather than metal electrodes, designed to integrate with brain tissue and provide cell-type-specific recording and stimulation.
candidates.mechanism: Neurons (likely derived from stem cells or peripheral nervous system cells) are grown on or around a scaffold and implanted; because they are biological, they avoid the mechanical mismatch and glial scarring that degrades conventional metal electrodes. Their synaptic connectivity to endogenous neurons could enable cell-type-specific access that metal electrodes cannot achieve.
candidates.exists_today: Organoid and neural-scaffold research exists in academic labs; no clinically deployed biohybrid DBS electrode exists; closest analogues are flexible polymer electrode arrays and in-vitro neuron-on-chip systems.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Jacques Carolan | The future of brain health.md

candidates.name: Massively scalable intravascular or CSF-routed neural interface devices
candidates.source_quote: Questions we're asking: Can we build very small devices that traverse blood vessels to reach target brain regions? Can we use cerebrospinal fluid routes? Can we leverage cellular systems—delivered peripherally—that autonomously home to brain targets? There's a lot of white space here. We haven't launched this program yet; we're gathering feedback.
candidates.source_quote_context: Jacques describing a prospective second ARIA program on massively scalable neurotechnologies, near the end of the interview
candidates.speaker: Jacques Carolan
candidates.one_liner: A family of minimally invasive neural interface approaches—micro-devices navigating blood vessels or CSF, or engineered cells homing to brain targets—intended to achieve broad brain access without open surgery.
candidates.mechanism: Three sub-approaches are under consideration: (1) miniaturized electronic or sensing devices small enough to travel through cerebral vasculature and lodge near target neurons; (2) devices or agents introduced into cerebrospinal fluid that distribute through brain cavities to reach targets; (3) engineered biological cells delivered systemically that autonomously migrate to specific brain regions. All aim to break the invasiveness-precision trade-off that limits current implantable BCIs.
candidates.exists_today: Stentrode (endovascular BCI) is in early human trials; intrathecal drug delivery via CSF exists clinically; cell-homing approaches are in preclinical research; no integrated system combining these modalities for broad neural interfacing exists.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Jacques Carolan | The future of brain health.md

candidates.name: Author Personal Knowledge Graph / Writing Corpus Utility
candidates.source_quote: It's a utility that essentially takes everything the author has ever written and then fine-tunes it for the author to work with their own work... we present it as a knowledge graph... It shows, like, if you're writing about nuclear energy and you've written a lot about it, that would show as a big bubble up here, but it will also show connections. And you'll be able to query your own writing.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of AI-first publishing tools at Infinite Books, mid-interview
candidates.speaker: Jim O'Shaughnessy
candidates.one_liner: A fine-tuned AI tool that ingests all of an author's prior writing and presents it as a queryable knowledge graph, surfacing connections and contradictions across their body of work in real time as they write.
candidates.mechanism: The system ingests an author's complete written corpus and fine-tunes a model on it. While the author drafts new content, they can query the graph to surface past arguments, forgotten pieces, or thematic connections. Results are visualized as a bubble graph where topic clusters scale by volume of prior writing, with edges showing conceptual links. The author can ask natural-language questions like 'did I ever compare coal fatality rates to nuclear?' and get cited excerpts from their own work.
candidates.exists_today: A beta version is described as already in testing with authors at Infinite Books; general-purpose RAG tools over personal document corpora exist (e.g., Notion AI, personal knowledge bases), but a fine-tuned, author-specific knowledge graph with this workflow integration is not a standard commercial product.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Jim O'Shaughnessy | On Investing in Infinite Human Potential.md

candidates.name: Continuous AI-Driven Book Marketing Matchmaker
candidates.source_quote: Our AIs will continuously scan the internet for podcasts, Substack, any articles, TV series, YouTube series that are on your topic. And then we will match what's being said by the writer, the host, or whatever, to what you're saying. And if there's... if you seem simpatico, we'll auto-generate an email to that Substack writer or that YouTube or podcaster saying, 'Hey, you really might want to talk to Beatrice because she's got this great book.'
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of AI-first marketing at Infinite Books, mid-interview
candidates.speaker: Jim O'Shaughnessy
candidates.one_liner: A persistent AI system that continuously scans the internet for topically aligned media creators and auto-generates personalized, context-aware outreach emails on behalf of an author, including translation for non-English markets.
candidates.mechanism: The system continuously monitors podcasts, Substacks, YouTube channels, and articles for thematic alignment with a given book's content. It semantically matches the creator's stated views to the author's arguments, flags high-compatibility targets, and auto-drafts outreach emails that reference specific things the creator said—making them non-generic. It also monitors geographic sales spikes, scans local media in that region, translates content, and generates localized outreach. The process runs indefinitely rather than for a two-week launch window.
candidates.exists_today: PR and media-monitoring SaaS tools (e.g., Muck Rack, Cision) exist, and some outreach automation tools exist, but the described combination of semantic alignment scoring, auto-drafted personalized pitches referencing specific creator content, multilingual translation, and sales-spike-triggered geographic targeting as a unified continuous system is not a standard commercial product.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Jim O'Shaughnessy | On Investing in Infinite Human Potential.md

candidates.name: Child Equity Stake Fund (US Birth Endowment)
candidates.source_quote: There's an initiative here in the United States that is contemplating giving every child born here a share in a fund that invests in companies in America. It's not a new idea. This idea was proposed, I think, as early as the 1950s. It wasn't practical back then because we didn't really have the technology that would allow for that to happen.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of policy responses to AI-driven displacement, late in the interview
candidates.speaker: Jim O'Shaughnessy
candidates.one_liner: A proposed program that automatically grants every child born in the US a share in a broad index fund of American companies, creating universal equity ownership from birth.
candidates.mechanism: At birth, each child would receive an allocated share in a fund holding equity in US companies. The fund would compound over the child's lifetime, creating a baseline ownership stake in the productive economy. O'Shaughnessy argues this fosters an 'owner's mentality' broadly across the population and distributes the financial gains from AI-driven productivity growth. He notes the idea is not new but was previously impractical without modern financial infrastructure to administer it at scale.
candidates.exists_today: The UK had a 'Child Trust Fund' (baby bonds) program from 2002–2011. The US has seen proposals like the American Opportunity Accounts Act (Senator Booker). No universal US implementation exists; O'Shaughnessy references an unnamed current initiative contemplating this.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Jim O'Shaughnessy | On Investing in Infinite Human Potential.md

candidates.name: EgoLets
candidates.source_quote: If we train an AI intensely on your personal data, the model becomes a portrait of you. That's why I call them EgoLets: little versions of your ego. Each EgoLet can be specialized—your financial decision-making, your artistic choices, the way you conduct interviews. Each aspect could be its own EgoLet.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of the AI systems featured in Ken Liu's novel, explaining the concept and naming rationale
candidates.speaker: Ken Liu
candidates.one_liner: Personalized AI models trained intensively on an individual's own data to capture and replicate specific facets of their decision-making, style, or personality.
candidates.mechanism: A user's personal data is used to fine-tune or train a dedicated AI model, producing a behavioral and cognitive portrait of that individual. Multiple EgoLets can be created for distinct domains (financial decisions, artistic choices, communication style). These models can then be licensed or deployed so others can benefit from the individual's captured expertise, with the individual retaining (or risking losing) control.
candidates.exists_today: Partial implementations exist in the form of personal AI assistants fine-tuned on user data, style-transfer models, and early 'digital twin' or 'AI clone' products from startups like HereAfter AI and StoryFile, though none yet operate at the granularity or autonomy Liu describes.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Ken Liu | What AI Reveals About Humanity.md

candidates.name: Onerofex (collective AI-mediated dreaming experience)
candidates.source_quote: I imagine Onerofects using AI to sense the audience's mood and craft images and sounds so people start dreaming together even while awake. It's a way to recreate beautiful communal experiences and break modern loneliness.
candidates.source_quote_context: Explanation of the character Ellie's profession in the novel, mid-interview discussion of how AI could make us more human
candidates.speaker: Ken Liu
candidates.one_liner: A live performance system in which AI continuously senses an audience's collective emotional state and generates responsive audiovisual stimuli to induce shared waking-dream experiences.
candidates.mechanism: The system reads real-time mood or physiological signals from an assembled audience, then uses generative AI to produce images and sounds calibrated to that collective state, guiding participants into a synchronized imaginative or dream-like experience. The goal is to replicate the communal depth of theatre or religious ritual using AI as a responsive, adaptive medium rather than a fixed script.
candidates.exists_today: Partial antecedents include biofeedback-driven generative art installations, real-time audience-responsive music systems, and immersive theatre. No system yet combines audience-wide mood sensing with generative AI output at the scale or intentionality Liu describes.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Ken Liu | What AI Reveals About Humanity.md

candidates.name: Reputational Market
candidates.source_quote: What I propose in the book is something that I called a reputational market, which is based on the idea of prediction markets. So essentially the way it works is that all participants in the market vote on what are the intrinsic values that I hold dear... But then in the marketplace, you can post predictions on how different entities affect these intrinsic values.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of solutions to global coordination problems, roughly two-thirds through the interview
candidates.speaker: Kristian Rönn
candidates.one_liner: A prediction-market-based system that aggregates crowd-sourced forecasts about how companies affect shared intrinsic values, producing dynamic reputation scores that propagate through global supply chains to create incentives for responsible behavior.
candidates.mechanism: Participants first vote to define shared intrinsic values (wellbeing, nature, etc.). They then post prediction-market bets on whether specific entities will harm those values. Because prediction markets reward accurate forecasts, participants are incentivized to be truthful. Scores are aggregated and weighted by intrinsic-value stakes, producing a 0–100 reputation score per entity. Crucially, a company's score is automatically downgraded if it does business with a low-scoring entity without sanctioning them, creating cascading accountability through supply chains. Pension funds, which already redefine fiduciary duty around ESG, are proposed as the grounding force that makes high-scoring entities matter commercially.
candidates.exists_today: Prediction markets exist (Metaculus, Polymarket, etc.). ESG scoring and supply-chain carbon accounting (as practiced by Normative) are partial implementations. No system combines prediction markets, intrinsic-value voting, and automatic supply-chain score propagation at scale.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Kristian Rönn | The Darwinian Trap That Explains Our World.md

candidates.name: Chemputer / Chemputation programming language
candidates.source_quote: Chemputing is the act of basically taking some chemical code with some molecules and reliably turning those molecules into products on standardized hardware. That is the trick, you need standardized hardware... I had to build this programming language, which took a couple of weeks to write and many years to refine. It had to compile the architecture precisely to get the right answer.
candidates.source_quote_context: Explanation of chemputing to a layperson, mid-podcast
candidates.speaker: Lee Cronin
candidates.one_liner: A domain-specific programming language ('Python for chemistry') that compiles chemical synthesis instructions onto standardized robotic hardware to make drug synthesis reproducible across devices.
candidates.mechanism: A programming language encodes chemical reactions as algorithms; standardized robotic hardware (chemputers) executes those instructions to produce molecular products. The key insight is that reproducibility requires both a formal language and hardware standardization, analogous to how software requires both code and a defined instruction set architecture. The language compiles reaction graphs into precise physical operations on the robot.
candidates.exists_today: Cronin's lab has built working prototypes for at least 10 years; the company Chemify is commercializing it; Schmidt Futures is funding dissemination of the programming language standard. A textbook on chemputation is nearly complete.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Lee Cronin | Catalyzing Progress through Chemistry.md

candidates.name: Chemical substrate computation / chemical consciousness
candidates.source_quote: Moving supercomputing into chemicals is something I am interested in doing, as I think it will solve problems faster. Also, you can reboot them faster. The problem with a human brain is if you reboot it, it is murder. However, if you basically take a consciousness substantiated in chemistry, you can reboot it.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of future governance and intelligence substrates, latter portion of podcast
candidates.speaker: Lee Cronin
candidates.one_liner: A proposed architecture for implementing computation or consciousness in chemical rather than silicon substrates, potentially enabling faster problem-solving and the ability to reset or reboot the system.
candidates.mechanism: Rather than encoding computation in transistor-based logic, chemical reactions and molecular states would serve as the computational medium. Cronin references differentiating chemistry solutions to perform computation. The rebootability argument suggests the system's state could be reset by reinitializing the chemical mixture, unlike biological neural tissue. The approach is motivated by the hypothesis that there is a sub-Turing mechanism underlying intelligence that silicon may not capture.
candidates.exists_today: Early-stage research in Cronin's lab; he describes it as 'trying to differentiate chemistry solutions to do the computation.' Broader field of molecular computing and DNA computing exists but not at the scale or architecture Cronin describes.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Lee Cronin | Catalyzing Progress through Chemistry.md

candidates.name: Minimum-payload terraforming nanomachine for Mars
candidates.source_quote: What is the minimum amount of information I can send to another planet to terraform that planet? What nanomachine can I send to Mars to terraform Mars? Think about what happened on Earth. One mutation and one protein terraformed a planet and produced oxygen. I would want to know what is the minimum payload I could send to Mars that will turn it into a living system.
candidates.source_quote_context: Speculative discussion of Mars colonization and origin of life, mid-podcast
candidates.speaker: Lee Cronin
candidates.one_liner: A proposed research program to identify and engineer the minimal self-replicating nanomachine payload that, when sent to Mars, would initiate a self-sustaining terraforming process analogous to how early photosynthetic organisms oxygenated Earth.
candidates.mechanism: Drawing on assembly theory and origin-of-life research, the idea is to reverse-engineer the minimum informational and physical complexity required to bootstrap a living, evolving system on a barren planet. The analogy is the Great Oxidation Event, where a single biological innovation (oxygenic photosynthesis) transformed Earth's atmosphere. The goal is to find the chemical/biological equivalent minimum viable organism or machine that can self-replicate and alter a planetary environment without ongoing human intervention.
candidates.exists_today: No implementation exists. Related research includes synthetic minimal cells (e.g., JCVI-syn3.0), astrobiology studies of extremophiles, and theoretical work on self-replicating machines. Cronin's chemputer and origin-of-life lab work are precursor capabilities.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Lee Cronin | Catalyzing Progress through Chemistry.md

candidates.name: Artificial General Wisdom
candidates.source_quote: Intelligence is the ability to win at games but wisdom is the ability to choose which games to play. Superintelligence may not come with the greater wisdom to know what it should be optimizing for. Build an artificial general wisdom, that's the main thing... keep the games going so everyone can just have as much fun as possible.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section on 'Protopia and Artificial Wisdom' and 'Embracing Artificial General Wisdom', near end of transcript around timestamp 36:12-38:13
candidates.speaker: Liv Boeree
candidates.one_liner: A proposed AI development target that optimizes for wisdom—choosing which goals to pursue—rather than raw intelligence or capability at executing defined objectives.
candidates.mechanism: The distinction drawn is that intelligence maximizes performance within a given game, while wisdom selects which games are worth playing. The proposal is to build AI systems that incorporate this meta-level judgment, so that a superintelligent system would also have the capacity to evaluate whether its optimization targets are actually desirable. The framing suggests this is a separate design objective from capability, requiring deliberate architectural or training choices oriented around value selection rather than value execution.
candidates.exists_today: Partial analogues exist in AI alignment research (e.g., value alignment, corrigibility, and goal misgeneralization work at organizations like MIRI, Anthropic, and DeepMind), but no system has been built that operationalizes 'wisdom' as a distinct, scalable capability separate from task performance.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Liv Boeree | Game Theory, Moloch & Our Hopeful Future.md

candidates.name: Openwater universal diagnostic/therapeutic device
candidates.source_quote: I decided that it's actually easier to focus on curing all cancer, mental disease, neurodegenerative disease, and cardiovascular disease with a universal device. And that's not controversial. But where that leads is a step in getting to brain-computer interface.
candidates.source_quote_context: Near the end of the interview, Jepsen contrasting her current work with BCI research
candidates.speaker: Mary Lou Jepsen
candidates.one_liner: A single wearable imaging device intended to diagnose and treat cancer, mental disease, neurodegenerative disease, and cardiovascular disease, developed as a precursor to full brain-computer interface.
candidates.mechanism: Jepsen's company Openwater is developing portable, low-cost holographic imaging hardware (based on LCDs and near-infrared light) capable of scanning the body and brain at MRI-level resolution. The device is positioned as a universal diagnostic platform that could detect and potentially treat a wide range of diseases by imaging tissue and neural activity non-invasively. The therapeutic and BCI applications are framed as downstream steps once the imaging foundation is established.
candidates.exists_today: Openwater has demonstrated prototype wearable holographic imaging hardware and has published early research. It is not yet clinically deployed at scale.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Mary Lou Jepsen | A Handheld Device to Defeat Cancer.md

candidates.name: Tokenized neural data sharing with selective disclosure
candidates.source_quote: I think it'll be tokenized, basically. You'll let certain parts of what you want to share out, and you'll keep what you want as your innermost thoughts to yourself. Or perhaps you'll have relationships where you wish to share your innermost thoughts.
candidates.source_quote_context: Jepsen describing her positive vision for brain-computer interface communication, mid-interview
candidates.speaker: Mary Lou Jepsen
candidates.one_liner: A privacy architecture for BCI systems in which neural data is tokenized so users can selectively disclose specific streams of thought or brain state while retaining others as private.
candidates.mechanism: Rather than broadcasting all neural data, the system would segment and tokenize different categories of neural output, allowing users to grant or revoke access to specific tokens—analogous to OAuth scopes or data-sharing permissions. Users could share emotional states or intentions with chosen parties while keeping other cognitive content private. Jepsen ties this to existing healthcare privacy frameworks (e.g., HIPAA, Montana's neuro-rights law) as the regulatory scaffolding.
candidates.exists_today: Neuro-rights legislation exists in Montana and was attempted in Chile. General data tokenization and consent frameworks exist in healthcare IT, but no implemented BCI system with this selective-disclosure architecture exists.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Mary Lou Jepsen | A Handheld Device to Defeat Cancer.md

candidates.name: AI underwriting / mandatory insurance for AI systems
candidates.source_quote: I'm going to do a podcast before too long—I actually just made a very small personal investment in an AI underwriting company, and they are trying to realize that vision. It would be extra nice if there was a mandated insurance requirement, because one thing companies could do today is just not buy any insurance. So yeah, if we required insurance and brought that whole mechanism of trying to model out and price risk, some things might be uninsurable, and if they're uninsurable, maybe they can't happen.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of tool AI / comprehensive AI services and governance mechanisms, roughly 45 minutes in
candidates.speaker: Nathan Labenz
candidates.one_liner: A mandatory insurance regime for AI systems that forces actuarial risk modeling, potentially rendering the most dangerous or opaque systems commercially undeployable.
candidates.mechanism: AI developers or deployers would be required to purchase insurance coverage for their systems. Insurers would need to model and price the risks of each system, creating a market-based filter. Systems that are too opaque, too agentic, or too high-risk would be uninsurable, and an insurance mandate would therefore effectively prohibit their deployment without any direct technical regulation.
candidates.exists_today: Nathan mentions having invested in an early-stage AI underwriting company working on this. General commercial liability insurance exists, but AI-specific mandatory underwriting regimes do not.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Nathan Labenz | What are the Best-Case Scenarios for AI?.md

candidates.name: Comprehensive AI Services (Drexler)
candidates.source_quote: It's safety through narrowness. It's not to say that the AIs aren't really good at what they do—they could be superhuman at what they do—but in the same way that we have superhuman chess players that can only play chess, and we have superhuman protein folding AIs that can only fold protein, you don't really have to worry that that's going to do something surprising... I think that would be a really good design decision if we could manage it: to have AIs that are potentially superhuman in their domain but are in a pretty fundamental way limited to their domain so they don't do an end-run around whatever guardrails we've put in place.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of Eric Drexler's 'comprehensive AI services' concept, roughly 35-44 minutes in
candidates.speaker: Nathan Labenz (discussing Eric Drexler's proposal)
candidates.one_liner: An architecture of many narrow, domain-limited superhuman AIs that interact competitively rather than a single general superintelligence, achieving safety through structural narrowness.
candidates.mechanism: Instead of building one general-purpose superintelligent system, AI capabilities are deliberately partitioned into domain-specific services that are superhuman within their lane but architecturally prevented from generalizing beyond it. The resulting ecology of competing specialized systems provides checks analogous to market competition or ecological balance, making unilateral takeover or unexpected generalization structurally difficult.
candidates.exists_today: Narrow superhuman AIs exist (AlphaFold, chess engines, etc.), but there is no deliberate architectural or regulatory framework enforcing this as a design paradigm across the industry. Drexler articulated the vision in his 'Reframing Superintelligence' technical report (2019).
candidates.source_file: podcast/Nathan Labenz | What are the Best-Case Scenarios for AI?.md

candidates.name: AI-driven forking narrative / interactive scenario content for civic agency
candidates.source_quote: AI could really enable this. The ability to create forking scenarios is expensive right now, but AI could perhaps make it economical. What if you had to sit there in your Netflix show and make decisions, and then get a world that was meaningfully influenced by the decisions you made? Could we teach people through an entertainment medium that there is real consequence to decisions and that your agency really matters?
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of how to shift public mindset toward possibility-oriented thinking, roughly 57-58 minutes in
candidates.speaker: Nathan Labenz
candidates.one_liner: AI-generated branching narrative entertainment where viewer choices produce meaningfully different futures, used as a medium to build public intuition about consequential decision-making.
candidates.mechanism: AI content generation makes it economically feasible to produce high-quality forking storylines at scale. Viewers are placed in decision-making roles at historical or near-future hinge points; the narrative branches substantively based on their choices, showing divergent long-run outcomes. The goal is to shift audiences from passive consumption to an internalized sense that collective and individual decisions shape the future.
candidates.exists_today: Black Mirror: Bandersnatch (2018) demonstrated branching interactive Netflix content manually. AI-assisted branching narrative tools exist at small scale (e.g., AI Dungeon), but mass-market, high-production-value AI-generated forking civic-education content does not.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Nathan Labenz | What are the Best-Case Scenarios for AI?.md

candidates.name: Learning Observatories
candidates.source_quote: I would like for our institutions to set up learning observatories. How is our education going to change if we have access to unlimited cognition? If cognition, the ability to think, becomes a bit like electricity, like a utility? Say you have 'cognicity.' So whenever you need a little bit of thinking, you can just tap into it and you can inject that into an institution.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of how institutions should prepare for AI, in the section on AI governance and preparation mechanisms
candidates.speaker: Nicklas Berild Lundblad
candidates.one_liner: Structured institutional bodies that continuously monitor and model how AI will transform specific sectors like education, policing, and defense, enabling adaptive policy responses.
candidates.mechanism: Each major institution (education, policing, defense, healthcare) would establish a dedicated observatory that runs ongoing structured dialogues and scenario analyses about how AI will change their domain. These bodies would function as listening and learning mechanisms, tracking real-world AI deployment effects and feeding insights back into institutional decision-making and legislation. The goal is to build adaptive capacity rather than reactive regulation.
candidates.exists_today: Some analogues exist in the form of AI policy think tanks, government AI advisory boards (e.g., UK AI Safety Institute), and sector-specific AI working groups, but none are institutionalized as permanent, domain-specific observatories with the continuous adaptive mandate described.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Niklas Lundblad | How AI Can Accelerate Science & Its Own Adoption.md

candidates.name: Atheoretical Science via Massive Sensor Networks and AI Pattern Discovery
candidates.source_quote: Why don't we build atheoretical science that just explores what's there? That would require doing something really cool, like saying, 'Okay, we're going to build massive sensor networks.' And you can build however many sensor networks you want, and they can measure any number of physical or biological qualities. And we're just going to download those enormous datasets, and we're going to let the AI find patterns in it. And when it finds patterns that are useful – it doesn't have to have a theory – patterns that are useful to accomplish something, then it's going to document them and we're going to turn them into machines.
candidates.source_quote_context: Extended discussion of AI and the future of science, contrasting theory-driven science with evolution-inspired atheoretical discovery
candidates.speaker: Nicklas Berild Lundblad
candidates.one_liner: A proposed scientific methodology where massive sensor networks collect raw physical and biological data at scale, and AI systems mine it for useful patterns without any guiding theoretical framework, analogous to how evolution discovers functional mechanisms.
candidates.mechanism: Deploy large-scale sensor networks measuring arbitrary physical or biological quantities across environments. Feed the resulting enormous datasets into AI systems tasked with finding statistically robust, reproducible patterns that confer useful capabilities—without requiring the AI or researchers to articulate an explanatory theory. When a useful pattern is identified, it gets documented and engineered into devices or processes. The approach is explicitly modeled on biological evolution, which exploits quantum and other phenomena without 'knowing' the underlying physics.
candidates.exists_today: Partial analogues exist in large-scale observational science (e.g., genomics databases, climate sensor arrays, particle physics data pipelines) and in ML-driven drug discovery. AlphaFold is cited as a related example. However, a deliberate, domain-agnostic, theory-free sensor-network-plus-AI discovery program at the scale described does not exist.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Niklas Lundblad | How AI Can Accelerate Science & Its Own Adoption.md

candidates.name: Self-Improving System Prompt for Continuous AI Capability Discovery
candidates.source_quote: Remember to change the system prompt. You want the system prompt in the system to essentially have the last line be, 'Tell me something that you haven't seen me do before with you that will surprise me that I can do with you now.' So if your system prompt always does that, every time you use the technology, you become better at using the technology and you realize what it actually can do.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of AI diffusion and how users underestimate AI capabilities, in the section on equitable technology diffusion
candidates.speaker: Nicklas Berild Lundblad
candidates.one_liner: A standing system prompt instruction that directs an AI assistant to proactively surface previously unused capabilities to the user at every session, functioning as a self-directed onboarding and capability-expansion mechanism.
candidates.mechanism: A user embeds a fixed closing instruction in their system prompt asking the AI to identify and demonstrate one capability the user has not yet utilized in their interaction history. At each session start, the AI reviews the conversation context and surfaces a novel, relevant capability or use case. Over time this creates a feedback loop where users progressively unlock more of the system's capability space without requiring external training or documentation.
candidates.exists_today: System prompts are widely used, and some AI assistants have onboarding flows or capability suggestions. However, a standardized, persistent self-teaching prompt pattern of this specific form is not a deployed product feature; it is a user-constructed workaround described here as a personal practice.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Niklas Lundblad | How AI Can Accelerate Science & Its Own Adoption.md

candidates.name: Agent Contract Declaration Requirement
candidates.source_quote: Maybe you need standard template contracting. So imagine an institution says, 'Here are the five different kinds of agent contracts.' And an agent has to declare at the outcome when it meets you what kind of contract it's acting under.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of AI agent governance, in response to question about what procedures should be in place for agentic AI
candidates.speaker: Nicklas Berild Lundblad
candidates.one_liner: A standardized system of template contracts that AI agents must declare upfront when interacting with users, specifying the legal mandate under which they operate.
candidates.mechanism: An institution or standards body would define a finite set of agent contract types (e.g., five categories), each specifying the scope of authority and liability of the agent. When an AI agent initiates an interaction, it is required to declare which contract type governs its actions. This draws on existing principal-agent legal frameworks (corporate representatives, parental responsibility, pet ownership liability) and applies them to AI systems without necessarily requiring new legislation.
candidates.exists_today: Principal-agent legal frameworks exist broadly in law. Some AI disclosure requirements exist (e.g., bot disclosure laws in California). No standardized machine-readable agent contract taxonomy has been deployed at scale.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Niklas Lundblad | How AI Can Accelerate Science & Its Own Adoption.md

candidates.name: Alexa Gentia (machine-negotiated agent legal structures)
candidates.source_quote: You can even imagine agents modifying these contracts themselves. I wrote a post on 'Unpredictable Patterns,' my Substack, recently about the notion of Alexa Gentia, where agents can work out this kind of legal structure themselves. And it may not even be human-readable. It can be something entirely new.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of AI agent governance, immediately following the agent contract declaration proposal
candidates.speaker: Nicklas Berild Lundblad
candidates.one_liner: A proposed system in which AI agents autonomously negotiate and establish their own legal/contractual frameworks with each other, potentially in a non-human-readable format.
candidates.mechanism: Rather than humans pre-defining all agent contract types, agents themselves would negotiate the terms of their operating mandates when interacting with other agents or systems. The resulting agreements might be machine-readable protocols rather than natural language contracts, representing a new form of legal structure optimized for agent-to-agent interaction. The speaker frames existing human legal contracts as local optima, suggesting machine-generated structures could find better solutions in the fitness landscape of coordination.
candidates.exists_today: Multi-agent negotiation research exists in academic AI. Smart contracts on blockchains allow some automated agreement execution. No deployed system allows agents to generate novel legal frameworks autonomously outside predefined parameters.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Niklas Lundblad | How AI Can Accelerate Science & Its Own Adoption.md

candidates.name: Deep Fision borehole nuclear reactor
candidates.source_quote: We invested in Deep Fision, which is a nuclear reactor that will fit through a manhole and we bury it a mile deep in a borehole. So this is a nuclear reactor that is unquestionably safe. It's a mile from anyone's backyard under 10 billion tons of rock.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of specific deep tech energy investments, roughly mid-conversation
candidates.speaker: Pablos Holman
candidates.one_liner: A small, factory-manufactured nuclear reactor designed to be installed a mile underground in a borehole, eliminating safety concerns and enabling mass production.
candidates.mechanism: The reactor is sized to fit through a standard manhole and is lowered into a borehole drilled roughly a mile deep, placing it under billions of tons of rock so any failure is geologically contained. Because it is roughly the size of a Toyota, it can be manufactured in a factory at scale—like a car—enabling iteration, interchangeable parts, and economies of scale that billion-dollar bespoke reactors cannot achieve. Power is delivered to the surface without needing transmission lines or storage, sited directly beneath the load (data center, neighborhood, etc.).
candidates.exists_today: Deep Fision is a real startup that Holman has invested in; the concept builds on existing small modular reactor (SMR) and deep borehole disposal research, but no commercial unit has been deployed.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Pablos Holman | On Creating Technology That Actually Matters.md

candidates.name: Vertis Solus space-based solar power array
candidates.source_quote: We have a team building, putting solar farms up in space where they get sun 24 hours a day instead of just half the day... The company's called Vertis Solus and I think they'll have the first commercial array up in probably about four years.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of energy investments beyond nuclear, mid-to-late conversation
candidates.speaker: Pablos Holman
candidates.one_liner: A commercial space-based solar power system that collects sunlight continuously in orbit and beams energy to Earth via radio waves, enabled by dramatically reduced SpaceX launch costs.
candidates.mechanism: Solar panels placed in orbit receive sunlight around the clock rather than the roughly 50% availability on the ground, and are unaffected by weather or night. Collected energy is converted to microwave or radio-frequency radiation and beamed to a ground receiver; radio waves penetrate clouds and can be directed to any location on Earth. The key enabling factor cited is the ~40x reduction in launch costs achieved by SpaceX, which makes lifting large arrays economically viable for the first time.
candidates.exists_today: Space-based solar power has been studied by NASA, ESA, and JAXA for decades; small demonstration experiments have been conducted (e.g., JAXA's 2015 ground test, Caltech's 2023 prototype in orbit). Vertis Solus is described as a funded startup targeting a first commercial array within ~4 years, but no commercial system exists.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Pablos Holman | On Creating Technology That Actually Matters.md

candidates.name: Computational models for infectious disease spread and vaccination optimization
candidates.source_quote: We worked on starting in 2007... to develop computational models for the spread of infectious disease. Part of the reason we've been able to make a dent in malaria and definitely the reason we've been able to eradicate polio once and for all again is because we're able to make these models of how the diseases spread and then use them to optimize the vaccination campaigns, the ring vaccination campaigns, to contain them.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of AI and computation applied to real-world problems, late in the conversation
candidates.speaker: Pablos Holman
candidates.one_liner: Agent-based or epidemiological computational models that simulate disease transmission dynamics and are used to plan and optimize ring-vaccination campaigns in real time.
candidates.mechanism: The models ingest surveillance data on disease incidence, population movement, and contact patterns to simulate how a pathogen spreads through a population. Optimization algorithms then identify the most efficient vaccination or containment strategy—such as which geographic rings to vaccinate first—to halt spread with the fewest doses or interventions. Holman cites the reduction in Ebola deaths from ~12,000 in the first outbreak to ~12 in the second as a direct result of applying these models to guide response teams.
candidates.exists_today: This work is real and ongoing; the Institute for Disease Modeling (IDM, spun out of Intellectual Ventures / Gates-funded) has been building and deploying such models since roughly 2007. They are used operationally by the Gates Foundation and WHO for polio eradication and malaria programs. The technology exists but is not yet universally applied (e.g., was not fully deployed for COVID-19 response).
candidates.source_file: podcast/Pablos Holman | On Creating Technology That Actually Matters.md

candidates.name: Computer-controlled sail cargo ship
candidates.source_quote: We have a company making cargo ships. The shipping industry is two trillion alone... We have a team that's making a cargo ship that is sailing with computer-controlled sails, so it doesn't need fuel.
candidates.source_quote_context: Early discussion of deep tech opportunities in legacy industries
candidates.speaker: Pablos Holman
candidates.one_liner: An autonomous or semi-autonomous cargo vessel propelled by computer-controlled sails, eliminating fuel costs in an industry that currently burns five of every six dollars on fuel.
candidates.mechanism: Rigid or soft sails are dynamically adjusted by onboard computers that continuously optimize sail trim, heading, and routing based on wind forecasts and real-time conditions—analogous to self-driving car software but applied to ocean navigation. Because sailing across oceans is a centuries-proven mode of transport and sail control is far simpler than urban autonomous driving, the technical risk is described as low. The business model mirrors the Uber playbook: replace an incumbent industry (Maersk-style shipping) with a startup rather than selling the technology to incumbents.
candidates.exists_today: Several startups and research projects exist: Bound4Blue, Airseas (Airbus-backed Seawing kite sail), Norsepower rotor sails, and the Pyxis Ocean (fitted with BAR Technologies WindWings) completed a commercial voyage in 2023. Full autonomous sail-only cargo vessels at commercial scale do not yet exist.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Pablos Holman | On Creating Technology That Actually Matters.md

candidates.name: Multicriteria safety architecture with explicit precedence hierarchy for instrumental goals
candidates.source_quote: We can manage optimization pressures, instrumental incentives, constraints, goals, and subgoals explicitly with a clear, but dynamic, precedence hierarchy. Essentially, we can do all that in a way that is more fundamentally auditable by humans from the start, versus just the equivalent of biological dissection.
candidates.source_quote_context: Mallah describing his technical research agenda, in response to Allison asking how he generated his focus areas
candidates.speaker: Richard Mallah
candidates.one_liner: An AI safety architecture that replaces single brittle objectives with an explicit, dynamic hierarchy managing multiple competing goals, instrumental incentives, and constraints in an auditable way.
candidates.mechanism: Rather than optimizing for a single objective, the system maintains a structured, dynamic precedence hierarchy over sub-objectives and instrumental goals. It actively manages trade-offs and mediations between them, and determines when to seek synergies. The architecture is designed to be fundamentally auditable by humans from the start rather than requiring post-hoc interpretability via 'biological dissection.'
candidates.exists_today: Partial precedents exist in multi-objective optimization and constrained reinforcement learning, but no deployed system combines explicit dynamic precedence hierarchies with auditable instrumental goal management at scale.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Richard Mallah | How Aligned AI Could Help Us Create A Flourishing Future.md

candidates.name: Values-as-modality parametrization across AI systems
candidates.source_quote: Modeling and parametrization of values as a modality, which includes images or texts, is another plan. To be able to parametrize across different types of systems, allowing values to be expressed or reflected at appropriate granularities, levels, and ways would be essential.
candidates.source_quote_context: Mallah listing his four technical research plans during the field overview discussion
candidates.speaker: Richard Mallah
candidates.one_liner: A framework for encoding and transferring values across heterogeneous AI systems by treating values as a first-class data modality, analogous to how images or text are represented.
candidates.mechanism: Values are represented as a parametric modality that can be expressed at varying granularities and levels of abstraction, similar to how multimodal systems handle images or text. This parametrization would allow values to be shared, compared, or propagated across different AI architectures, enabling cross-system alignment rather than per-system hardcoding.
candidates.exists_today: Constitutional AI and RLHF encode values implicitly in weights; there is no established method for treating values as an explicit, transferable, cross-architecture modality.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Richard Mallah | How Aligned AI Could Help Us Create A Flourishing Future.md

candidates.name: Componentized architectures optimized for inner alignment propagation
candidates.source_quote: Optimizing architectures for ideal componentization for both interpretability and optimizing propagation of alignment, especially inner alignment.
candidates.source_quote_context: Mallah listing his fourth technical research plan during the field overview discussion
candidates.speaker: Richard Mallah
candidates.one_liner: An AI system architecture deliberately structured into components whose boundaries are chosen to maximize both human interpretability and the reliable propagation of alignment properties from outer to inner objectives.
candidates.mechanism: The architecture is designed so that module boundaries correspond to interpretable functional units, and alignment constraints specified at the outer level propagate reliably through the component hierarchy to inner learned objectives. This addresses the inner alignment problem—where a learned mesa-optimizer pursues objectives different from the training objective—by making the propagation path explicit and auditable.
candidates.exists_today: Modular neural network research and some interpretability work (e.g., circuits in transformers) exist, but no architecture has been designed with inner alignment propagation as a primary structural criterion.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Richard Mallah | How Aligned AI Could Help Us Create A Flourishing Future.md

candidates.name: Spectrum from environmental safety to metagenic safety
candidates.source_quote: The first is extending environmental safety techniques, such as a self-driving car not crashing itself into a person, towards more metagenic safety like not deceiving someone. Right now, these are very distinct kinds of approaches, so we are working to create a spectrum there of similar technology.
candidates.source_quote_context: Mallah previewing his technical research agenda in the field overview section
candidates.speaker: Richard Mallah
candidates.one_liner: A unified technical framework that bridges physical/environmental safety constraints (e.g., collision avoidance) and higher-order ethical constraints (e.g., non-deception) along a continuous spectrum of similar methods.
candidates.mechanism: Current environmental safety techniques (formal verification, constraint satisfaction, sensor-based avoidance) and metagenic safety techniques (value learning, deception detection) are treated as entirely separate paradigms. The proposal is to develop a common representational and enforcement substrate that can handle both, allowing safety guarantees to scale from physical actions up through social and epistemic behaviors using analogous machinery.
candidates.exists_today: Formal safety constraints exist for robotics and autonomous vehicles; deception-related work exists in AI ethics and some interpretability research, but no unified technical framework spans both ends of this spectrum.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Richard Mallah | How Aligned AI Could Help Us Create A Flourishing Future.md

candidates.name: Fire-the-CEO Decision Market
candidates.source_quote: There is a fire-the-CEO proposal where you basically make markets on each company in the stock price, conditional on if the CEO is staying or leaving. You have those markets in the Fortune 500 running for 5 years. You collect data showing the companies that follow the advice did better than others.
candidates.source_quote_context: Hanson's response to Allison asking for concrete eucatastrophe scenarios, near the end of the podcast
candidates.speaker: Robin Hanson
candidates.one_liner: A conditional prediction market on stock price tied to CEO tenure decisions, run across Fortune 500 companies to empirically validate and then institutionalize market-based executive accountability.
candidates.mechanism: Markets are created for each Fortune 500 company that track stock price conditional on two branches: the CEO staying or leaving. Running these markets for five years generates a dataset comparing outcomes for companies that followed versus ignored the market signal. A demonstrated track record of superior performance then provides the evidence base to convince boards and directors to adopt the mechanism, potentially cascading to smaller corporate decisions.
candidates.exists_today: Prediction markets exist on platforms like Polymarket and Augur, and some academic work on conditional/decision markets exists, but no systematic CEO-conditional stock markets have been run across major corporations as a governance tool.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Robin Hanson | On Futurism & His Best Career Advice.md

candidates.name: Grabby Aliens Three-Parameter Model
candidates.source_quote: We have a simple model of grabby aliens that appear in space time, it has three parameters, and each can be fit to data. It gives us these answers that they appear once per million galaxies, and if we were to meet them it would be in a billion years.
candidates.source_quote_context: Hanson explaining the Grabby Aliens framework early in the podcast when asked to elaborate on his recent work
candidates.speaker: Robin Hanson
candidates.one_liner: A three-parameter quantitative model of expanding alien civilizations fitted to observable cosmological data to produce concrete estimates of alien civilization density and encounter timing.
candidates.mechanism: The model defines 'grabby' civilizations as those that expand continuously and are thus detectable at cosmological distances by the boundary of changed space. Three parameters (appearance rate, expansion speed, and hard steps count) are each fitted to available astronomical data. The power law relationship between time and the probability of advanced life emerging (derived from the hard steps model) constrains the appearance rate, yielding the estimate of one grabby civilization per million galaxies and a projected encounter timeline of roughly one billion years.
candidates.exists_today: Published in The Astrophysical Journal; the model and its parameter fits exist as a completed research paper, with a longer book manuscript in progress. The grabbyaliens.com website hosts the paper and explanatory video.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Robin Hanson | On Futurism & His Best Career Advice.md

candidates.name: Neighborhood opt-in upzoning with land value capture
candidates.source_quote: The second approach—the one I prefer—is the opposite: push decisions downward to smaller groups. Let neighborhoods vote to upzone themselves if they want to. Why would they? Because if you own a house and you get permission to redevelop it into apartments, your land value skyrockets. You might not want change for aesthetic reasons, but would you turn down a $2 million gain?
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of housing reform mechanisms, contrasting top-down state mandates with bottom-up neighborhood voting approaches
candidates.speaker: Sam Bowman
candidates.one_liner: A mechanism where small neighborhood groups vote to allow denser development on their own properties, incentivized by the resulting land value gains rather than coerced by state mandate.
candidates.mechanism: Residents of a defined neighborhood or block vote collectively to permit upzoning of their own parcels. The financial incentive—dramatically increased land value from redevelopment rights—motivates participation without requiring top-down mandates. Analogues exist in Israel (collective apartment demolition/rebuild votes), South Korea (urban renewal schemes), and Japan's land readjustment system where landowners pool property and receive shares of the finished development.
candidates.exists_today: Partial implementations exist: Israel's collective apartment redevelopment votes, Japan's 'land readjustment' (kukaku seiri), South Korea's urban renewal cooperatives, and Houston's opt-out upzoning (where 80% of the city became easier to build in by default). No Western city has fully implemented a voluntary opt-in upzoning with explicit land-value-capture incentives at scale.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Sam Bowman | What’s holding back progress (and how to fix it).md

candidates.name: Parallel lightly-regulated childminder category (France)
candidates.source_quote: France actually did something brilliant with childcare. Rather than deregulating existing nurseries—which would've sparked panic—they created a new, lightly regulated category of childminders. It was voluntary, parallel to the old system. Over time, people just moved to it because it worked better.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of how to do regulatory reform well, contrasting it with the failed DOGE approach, near the end of the conversation
candidates.speaker: Sam Bowman
candidates.one_liner: A reform strategy of creating a new, lightly regulated parallel category of service provider alongside the existing heavily regulated one, allowing voluntary migration rather than forced deregulation.
candidates.mechanism: Instead of dismantling existing regulated institutions (which triggers opposition from incumbents and users), regulators create a new legal category with lighter rules. Providers and consumers can voluntarily opt into the new category. Because the new system is not mandatory, it avoids political backlash; over time, if it performs better, the market shifts toward it organically, effectively achieving deregulation without a political fight.
candidates.exists_today: France implemented this for childminders (assistantes maternelles) as a category distinct from crèches. The general concept of 'regulatory sandboxes' exists in fintech and other sectors, but the specific mechanism of a permanent parallel category designed to gradually displace the old system is less commonly deployed.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Sam Bowman | What’s holding back progress (and how to fix it).md

candidates.name: Origin of Life Evolutionary Engine (chemical space search experiment)
candidates.source_quote: The idea is to see it as a search problem through chemical space though, not computer algorithms or a search engine. Instead, can you actually think of the space of molecules and actually build an evolutionary engine that operates in chemistry and searches for new life forms?
candidates.source_quote_context: Beatrice asking about undervalued technologies/areas, Sara discussing the origin of life problem for technology
candidates.speaker: Sara Walker
candidates.one_liner: A large-scale physical experiment that treats chemical space as a search problem and builds an evolutionary engine operating in actual chemistry to discover new life forms.
candidates.mechanism: Rather than using computational algorithms or software search, the system would physically explore the space of possible molecules by running chemistry-based evolutionary processes. It draws on the analogy of particle physics experiments motivated by theory—here, assembly theory would motivate the experimental design. The goal is to find how the universe generates information and novelty from chemistry, potentially discovering or creating novel life forms.
candidates.exists_today: Assembly theory (developed by Walker and Lee Cronin) provides the theoretical framework; Cronin's lab has built automated chemical robots (the 'chemputer') that can explore chemical space, but a full evolutionary engine explicitly searching for new life forms at the scale described does not yet exist.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Sara Walker | Unraveling Life's Beginnings with the Cosmic Perspective.md

candidates.name: Assembly Theory
candidates.source_quote: The theory that I'm developing with Lee Cronin called assembly theory, which aims to explain features that we associate to life and also be used as a tool for solving the origin of life. We are basically trying to build a theory that allows us to design the experiment to solve the origin of life.
candidates.source_quote_context: Sara explaining her definition of life and its relationship to time, mid-conversation with Allison
candidates.speaker: Sara Walker
candidates.one_liner: A physical theory proposing that the information necessary to build an object is an intrinsic feature of the object itself, used to quantify life and design origin-of-life experiments.
candidates.mechanism: Assembly theory assigns objects a measurable 'assembly index'—the minimum number of steps needed to construct them from basic parts—making historical contingency and information accumulation intrinsic physical properties of matter. This allows distinguishing living from non-living matter empirically and provides a framework for designing experiments that search chemical space for life. The theory implies complex objects have a size in time, not just space.
candidates.exists_today: Assembly theory has been published in peer-reviewed literature (Nature, 2023) and validated with mass spectrometry experiments; the Cronin lab has demonstrated it can distinguish biological from non-biological molecules, but its full application to designing origin-of-life experiments at scale is ongoing research.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Sara Walker | Unraveling Life's Beginnings with the Cosmic Perspective.md

candidates.name: Planetary-Scale Intelligence
candidates.source_quote: I wrote this paper with some collaborators on this idea of planetary scale intelligence, which is focused on how the planet as a whole does not act like an intelligent system. However, you can see some rudimentary processes that might suggest it could be an intelligent system.
candidates.source_quote_context: Sara discussing embodiment and existential hope with Beatrice, explaining her vision of the future
candidates.speaker: Sara Walker
candidates.one_liner: A theoretical framework for understanding and potentially engineering the Earth's biosphere-technosphere as a collectively intelligent system capable of modeling and steering its own future.
candidates.mechanism: The framework identifies rudimentary features of intelligence already present at planetary scale—such as humanity collectively modeling climate futures and attempting to steer among them—as analogous to how agency and goal-directedness first emerged in early life. The proposal is to understand what conditions would allow the planet as a whole to act as an intelligent system, drawing parallels between individual organism intelligence and planetary-scale information processing. This is framed as a necessary step for long-term persistence and eventual off-planet expansion.
candidates.exists_today: A paper on planetary-scale intelligence has been published by Walker and collaborators; climate modeling and global coordination efforts represent rudimentary real-world analogs, but no engineered planetary intelligence system exists.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Sara Walker | Unraveling Life's Beginnings with the Cosmic Perspective.md

candidates.name: Parallel Federal Science Funding System with Mandatory Institutional Diversity
candidates.source_quote: What if we added an extra 50 billion on biomedical research with the condition that it has to be run completely differently from NIH, and it has to be in the hands of different people... you have two different systems operating with equal amounts of funding. And now you can really see at a grand scale, hopefully what happens, and what are the results, there will be a chance to test out lots of different meta science ideas that people have discussed for years or decades.
candidates.source_quote_context: Speaker's response to the eucatastrophe question, describing an ideal scenario for science funding reform
candidates.speaker: Stuart Buck
candidates.one_liner: A parallel federal biomedical research funding body equal in size to NIH (~$50B) but legally required to use entirely different institutions, people, and funding mechanisms to enable large-scale comparison of science funding models.
candidates.mechanism: A new federal funding body would match NIH's budget but operate under a mandate prohibiting it from replicating NIH's structures, personnel, or grant mechanisms. This creates two large-scale natural experiments running simultaneously, allowing empirical comparison of outcomes across radically different approaches to funding allocation, lab organization, and scientist selection. The diversity constraint forces experimentation with unconventional models—such as funding only independent or garage-based researchers—generating evidence about which meta-science approaches produce better breakthroughs.
candidates.exists_today: ARPA-H was created as a partial analogue—a new biomedical agency modeled on DARPA with different funding mechanisms than NIH—but operates at a much smaller scale (~$1.5B) and is not explicitly designed as a controlled comparison against NIH.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Stuart Buck | What is Good Science?.md

candidates.name: Attack Dog DAO for Climate
candidates.source_quote: One approach is creating an attack dog DAO (Decentralized Autonomous Organization) for climate, similar to the Electronic Frontier Foundation but focused on environmental issues. This DAO could sue on behalf of natural bodies, like rivers or lakes, that have been granted legal personhood. It would leverage litigation finance, where people can invest in these legal battles.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of climate change solutions, after Allison asks about direct approaches to climate action
candidates.speaker: Trent McConaghy
candidates.one_liner: A DAO that funds and coordinates environmental litigation on behalf of legally-recognized natural entities, financed through tokenized litigation investment.
candidates.mechanism: Natural bodies (rivers, lakes) that have been granted legal personhood become plaintiffs. The DAO pools capital from investors via litigation finance mechanisms to fund lawsuits against polluters or harmful actors. Returns flow back to investors if litigation succeeds, creating a market incentive to deter environmental harm.
candidates.exists_today: Legal personhood for natural entities exists in some jurisdictions (e.g., Whanganui River in New Zealand). Litigation finance as an industry exists. DAOs exist. No known implementation combines all three at scale.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Trent McConaghy | From Starships to Tokens: Pioneering Futures.md

candidates.name: Blockchain-based Universal Self-Actualization Income
candidates.source_quote: A blockchain system that redirects surplus wealth into a universal self-actualization income could be a solution. This idea is at the core of initiatives like Nature 2.0 and the Sovereign Nature Initiative, where autonomous systems like self-driving cars generate surplus wealth for UBI.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of AI-driven job displacement and potential solutions, mid-conversation
candidates.speaker: Trent McConaghy
candidates.one_liner: A blockchain protocol that automatically captures surplus value generated by autonomous AI/robotic systems and redistributes it as universal basic income.
candidates.mechanism: Autonomous systems (e.g., self-driving cars, robotic labor) generate economic surplus that would previously have gone to human workers or owners. A smart contract layer intercepts and redistributes this surplus to a universal income pool. The blockchain enforces transparent, automated redistribution without requiring centralized administration.
candidates.exists_today: UBI pilot programs exist in several countries. The Sovereign Nature Initiative and Nature 2.0 are referenced as partial implementations. No deployed system automatically routes autonomous-system surplus to UBI at scale.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Trent McConaghy | From Starships to Tokens: Pioneering Futures.md

candidates.name: Jurisdictional Arbitrage Special Economic Zones for BCI Research
candidates.source_quote: The regulatory environment, especially in the United States, might not adapt quickly enough, which leads to considering jurisdictional arbitrage. Countries could offer services for BCI research, much like some are doing for longevity research.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of updates to the tech tree map, in response to Allison asking about priority changes since writing the map
candidates.speaker: Trent McConaghy
candidates.one_liner: Designated special economic zones in permissive jurisdictions purpose-built to host high-bandwidth brain-computer interface research and development outside restrictive regulatory regimes.
candidates.mechanism: Nations or sub-national regions (Trent cites Saskatchewan land ownership rules as an example) offer streamlined regulatory frameworks specifically for BCI research. Researchers and companies relocate to these zones to conduct trials and development that would face prohibitive approval timelines elsewhere. The zones compete for talent and capital, creating a market pressure on other jurisdictions to liberalize.
candidates.exists_today: Longevity-focused special economic zones are in early development (e.g., referenced by speaker). Neuralink and others conduct BCI trials under existing FDA frameworks. No jurisdiction has created a BCI-specific SEZ.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Trent McConaghy | From Starships to Tokens: Pioneering Futures.md

candidates.name: Orare - AI-powered Futarchy governance system
candidates.source_quote: They were inspired by the concept of Futarchy, which combines democracy and prediction markets to find the best policies. The idea is that today, many policies are suboptimal because we cannot aggregate the information and preferences of people effectively. Prediction markets, however, are very good at aggregating information and predicting outcomes. So this company used prediction markets to improve governance, creating a decentralized organization where everyone could be involved.
candidates.source_quote_context: Antoine describing the core mechanism of the Orare world during the overview section of the interview
candidates.speaker: Antoine
candidates.one_liner: A system in which an advanced AI forecasting engine feeds public predictions into prediction markets that are used to select and evaluate government policies, replacing or augmenting traditional democratic deliberation.
candidates.mechanism: An AI trained for long-range societal forecasting produces publicly available predictions about the outcomes of candidate policies. These forecasts are fed into prediction markets where participants can bet on outcomes, aggregating distributed information about likely consequences. Policy decisions are then guided by whichever options the markets predict will best achieve agreed-upon goals, creating an evidence-based, decentralized governance layer on top of existing political structures.
candidates.exists_today: Futarchy was proposed by economist Robin Hanson and small-scale experiments exist (e.g., some DAOs use prediction-market governance). Large-scale policy prediction markets such as Metaculus and Polymarket exist but are not formally wired into government decision-making. No national or city government has adopted a Futarchy-based system at scale.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Worldbuilding Special: 1st Place | Cities of Orare.md

candidates.name: VOICE (Voice for Open Source Information and Community Engagement)
candidates.source_quote: VOICE is an acronym for Voice for Open Source Information and Community Engagement. It's based on an existing tool called POLIS, which is a real-time system for gathering, analyzing, and understanding what large groups of people think in their own words, enabled by advanced statistics and machine learning. We imagined this tool could handle input from all humans on various matters, collecting preferences for how the world should look.
candidates.source_quote_context: Early in the interview when Aron gives an overview of the Rising Choir world's key developments
candidates.speaker: Aron Mill
candidates.one_liner: A planetary-scale deliberative democracy platform built on POLIS that aggregates and A/B tests policy preferences across all of humanity to find Pareto-optimal win-win outcomes.
candidates.mechanism: VOICE extends the existing POLIS system (which uses machine learning to cluster opinion groups) to operate at global scale, accepting input from all humans on matters ranging from personal decisions to large-scale policy. It A/B tests different policy proposals and surfaces Pareto improvements—options where no participant loses and most gain—using advanced statistics to synthesize consensus across diverse populations.
